lessons.title: SI Units and Prefixes
objectives: Name the SI units used in electrical engineering
Use the common prefixes (k, M, G, m, µ, n, p)
Convert values between prefixes safely
explain: Electrical values range from tiny (picofarads) to huge (megawatts). Prefixes keep numbers readable: 4700 Ω is written 4.7 kΩ.
Always check the prefix before you calculate. One wrong prefix changes a result by a factor of a thousand or a million.
lessons.definition: The SI system uses base and derived units. A prefix multiplies a unit by a power of ten. Units: coulomb (C) for charge, ampere (A) current, volt (V) voltage, ohm (Ω) resistance, watt (W) power, joule (J) energy, farad (F) capacitance, henry (H) inductance, hertz (Hz) frequency.

formulas.note: Giga, mega, kilo (capital M is mega, lower-case m is milli)
Milli, micro, nano, pico

formulas.f: value in base unit = number × prefix
formulas.note: For example 33 µF = 33 × 10⁻⁶ F

example.question: Convert 4.7 kΩ to ohms, 250 mA to amperes and 33 µF to farads.

applications: Transmission voltages are written in kV (for example 11 kV).
Insulation resistance readings are commonly in MΩ or GΩ.
Capacitors are rated in µF and nF; relay settings use amperes and seconds.
mistakes: Mixing M (mega) and m (milli): 1 MΩ and 1 mΩ differ by 10⁹.
Entering µF into a formula that needs farads.
Reading kW as kWh, or kVA as kW.
lessons.safety: A wrong prefix or unit on a drawing, rating or relay setting can lead to the wrong equipment or protection setting. Re-check units before you act on a number.

quiz.q: How many volts is 2 kV?
quiz.why: k means 10³, so 2 kV = 2000 V.

quiz.q: How many milliamperes is 0.5 A?
How many ohms is 1 MΩ?
quiz.why: M (mega) is 10⁶.

summary: Prefixes are powers of ten: k = 10³, M = 10⁶, m = 10⁻³, µ = 10⁻⁶.
Capital M is mega; lower-case m is milli.
Convert to base units before calculating.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Electric Charge and Current
lessons.prereq: None. This is the starting lesson.
objectives: Explain what electric charge is
Define current and the ampere
Use I = Q / t
Tell conventional current from electron flow
Connect an ammeter correctly
explain: Atoms contain protons (positive), electrons (negative) and neutrons (no charge). In a metal such as copper, some electrons are loosely held and can drift from atom to atom. These are free electrons.
Picture a water pipe: charge is the water, and current is how much water passes a point every second.
lessons.definition: Electric charge (Q) is a basic property of matter, measured in coulombs (C). Electric current (I) is the rate of flow of charge past a point, measured in amperes (A). One ampere is one coulomb per second.

formulas.note: I in amperes (A), Q in coulombs (C), t in seconds (s)
Charge moved equals current multiplied by time
One electron carries about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C

example.question: A current of 5 A flows through a cable for 2 minutes. How much charge moves through it?

applications: A clamp meter reads current from the magnetic field around a cable without opening the circuit.
A current transformer (CT) gives a protection relay a scaled-down copy of the line current.
mistakes: Mixing up electron flow and conventional current. Conventional current is defined from positive to negative; electrons move the opposite way.
Connecting an ammeter in parallel instead of in series.
Forgetting to convert units such as mA to A or minutes to seconds.
lessons.safety: Never open or touch a live circuit to measure current unless you are trained and your site procedure allows it. Use a properly rated meter and follow isolation rules.

quiz.q: What is the unit of electric charge?
quiz.why: Charge is measured in coulombs; the ampere is the unit of current.

quiz.q: 6 C passes a point in 3 s. What is the current?
How is an ammeter connected?
quiz.why: It has very low resistance, so it must sit in series with the circuit.

summary: Charge is in coulombs (C); current is in amperes (A).
I = Q / t, so 1 A = 1 C per second.
Conventional current flows from positive to negative.
Ammeters connect in series.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference
objectives: Define voltage (potential difference) and the volt
Explain the difference between EMF and terminal voltage
Use V = W / Q
Connect a voltmeter correctly
explain: In the water-pipe picture, voltage is the pressure difference that pushes the water. It always exists between two points, so we say voltage across a component, never through it.
A battery or generator acts like the pump: its EMF is the energy it gives to every coulomb of charge. A resistor or lamp uses up that energy, and the voltage across it is the potential difference.
lessons.definition: The potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving charge between them: V = W / Q. One volt is one joule per coulomb. The EMF (E) of a source is the energy it supplies per coulomb round the complete circuit. When a current I flows, the terminal voltage is lower than the EMF because of the internal resistance r of the source.

formulas.note: V in volts (V), W in joules (J), Q in coulombs (C)
Energy transferred when charge Q moves through potential difference V
Terminal voltage of a source with EMF E and internal resistance r

example.question: A battery has EMF 12 V and internal resistance 0.2 Ω. It supplies 5 A. (a) What is the terminal voltage? (b) How much energy is delivered to the external circuit when 30 C of charge passes through it?

applications: A voltmeter connected across a component shows the voltage the component uses.
A battery that reads 12 V with no load drops a little when it supplies a large current.
Substation control circuits are commonly powered from a DC battery supply, and its voltage under load matters for relays and trip coils.
mistakes: Connecting a voltmeter in series instead of across the component.
Saying "voltage through" a component. Voltage is across; current is through.
Treating EMF and terminal voltage as the same. They differ when current flows.
lessons.safety: Only measure voltage on energised equipment if you are trained, authorised and using a meter with the correct voltage and category rating for the installation.

quiz.q: What is one volt equal to?
quiz.why: V = W / Q, so a volt is a joule per coulomb.

quiz.q: 5 J of energy moves 2 C of charge between two points. What is the potential difference?
A 9 V source with internal resistance 1 Ω supplies 2 A. What is its terminal voltage?

summary: Voltage is energy per unit charge, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C).
Voltage is measured across two points, with the voltmeter in parallel.
Terminal voltage = EMF − I × r when current flows.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Resistance, Inductance and Capacitance
lessons.prereq: Ohm's Law; SI Units and Prefixes
objectives: Explain what resistance, inductance and capacitance do
Calculate the resistance of a conductor
Use the RC time constant
Calculate the energy stored in a capacitor
explain: A resistor turns electrical energy into heat. An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field and resists changes in current. A capacitor stores energy in an electric field and resists changes in voltage.
In a water system, a narrow pipe is resistance, a heavy flywheel is inductance (it resists changes in flow) and a flexible tank is capacitance (it resists changes in pressure).
lessons.definition: Resistance of a conductor: R = ρL / A, where ρ is the resistivity, L the length and A the cross-sectional area. An inductor of inductance L (henry) has v = L × di/dt and stores W = ½LI². A capacitor of capacitance C (farad) has Q = C × V, i = C × dv/dt and stores W = ½CV². The time constants are τ = RC and τ = L / R.

formulas.note: R in ohms, ρ in Ω·m, L in m, A in m². Resistance rises with length and falls with area

formulas.f: W = ½ C V²   W = ½ L I²
formulas.note: Energy in joules (J)

formulas.f: τ = R × C   τ = L / R
formulas.note: After 5τ the change is about 99 % complete

example.question: (a) Find the resistance of 100 m of copper cable of 2.5 mm² cross-section (take ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m). (b) Find the time constant of 10 kΩ with 100 µF. (c) Find the energy stored in a 100 µF capacitor charged to 230 V.

applications: Cable resistance sets the voltage drop and heating along a cable.
RC and RL time constants appear in timing circuits and in how fast currents build up.
Capacitors in power supplies and capacitor banks store energy that must be discharged safely.
mistakes: Using the diameter instead of the area in R = ρL / A.
Entering µF or mH without converting to farad or henry.
Assuming a capacitor is safe once the supply is off.
lessons.safety: A charged capacitor can give a shock after the supply is isolated. An inductor carrying current can produce a high voltage and an arc if the current is suddenly interrupted. Discharge, isolate and prove dead before working.

quiz.q: A conductor's length doubles (same material and area). What happens to its resistance?
quiz.why: R = ρL / A, so R is proportional to L.

quiz.q: What is the time constant of 1 kΩ and 10 µF?
Where does an inductor store its energy?
quiz.why: An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.

summary: R = ρL / A; τ = RC or L / R.
Capacitor energy = ½CV²; inductor energy = ½LI².
Resistors dissipate energy; inductors and capacitors store it.

practice.q: Find the resistance of 50 m of copper wire of 1.5 mm² (ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m).
Find the energy stored in a 470 µF capacitor at 12 V.

refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Ohm's Law
lessons.prereq: Electric Charge and Current; Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference
objectives: State Ohm's law
Rearrange V = I × R
Solve simple numerical problems
Know where Ohm's law does not apply
explain: Think of a water pipe: voltage is the pressure, current is the flow, and resistance is how narrow or rough the pipe is. For the same pressure, a narrower pipe gives less flow.
For many conductors at constant temperature, current rises in direct proportion to voltage.
lessons.definition: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the voltage across it, provided temperature and other physical conditions stay constant. The constant of proportionality is the resistance R, measured in ohms (Ω).

formulas.note: V in volts (V), I in amperes (A), R in ohms (Ω)
Current for a given voltage and resistance
Resistance from measured voltage and current

example.question: A heater element on a 230 V supply draws 5 A. What is its resistance?

applications: Choosing a resistor to limit current through an LED.
Estimating the current an element draws from its resistance and supply voltage.
mistakes: Using milliamps without converting: 20 mA is 0.02 A.
Assuming Ohm's law holds for every device. Diodes and lamp filaments are non-ohmic: their resistance changes with voltage or temperature.
lessons.safety: Practise with batteries or low-voltage supplies. Never experiment on mains wiring without qualified supervision and proper isolation.

quiz.q: A 12 V supply drives 0.5 A through a resistor. What is R?
Voltage doubles and resistance stays the same. What happens to the current?
quiz.why: I = V / R, so current is proportional to voltage.

summary: V = I × R, with V in volts, I in amperes, R in ohms.
Current is proportional to voltage at constant resistance.
Ohm's law holds for ohmic conductors at constant temperature.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Power and Energy
lessons.prereq: Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference; Ohm's Law
objectives: Define power and energy and their units
Use P = V × I, P = I²R and P = V²/R
Convert between joules and kilowatt-hours
Estimate the energy used by a load
explain: Power tells you how fast energy is being used. A 2 kW heater uses energy twice as fast as a 1 kW heater. Energy is the total used over time: run the heater for longer and you use more.
Think of power as the flow rate of a tap and energy as the amount of water in the bucket.
lessons.definition: Power (P) is the rate of transfer of energy, measured in watts: 1 W = 1 J/s. Energy (E) is the power multiplied by the time, measured in joules. Electricity is billed in kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

formulas.note: P in watts (W), V in volts (V), I in amperes (A)
Use whichever form matches the values you know (resistive load)
E in kWh when P is in kW and t is in hours
Conversion between the billing unit and the SI unit

example.question: A heating element has a resistance of 46 Ω and is connected to 230 V. Find its power and the energy it uses in 3 hours.

applications: Energy meters measure kilowatt-hours.
The I²R heating in a cable is why cables have current ratings.
Equipment nameplates state power so the supply and protection can be chosen.
mistakes: Confusing W (power) with Wh or kWh (energy).
Mixing kW with kVA. They are different quantities for AC loads.
Using P = V × I for an AC motor without the power factor.
lessons.safety: Never load a cable, plug or heater beyond its rating. Excess current causes overheating and fire risk, which is what fuses and breakers protect against.

quiz.q: A load takes 5 A from 230 V (resistive). What is its power?
A 2 kW heater runs for 5 hours. How much energy does it use?
The current in a fixed resistor doubles. What happens to the power?
quiz.why: P = I²R, so doubling I multiplies P by 4.

summary: Power is energy per second; 1 W = 1 J/s.
P = V × I = I²R = V²/R for a resistive load.
Energy = power × time; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Algebra, Trigonometry and Phasor Basics
lessons.prereq: Ohm's Law; SI Units and Prefixes
objectives: Rearrange formulas without changing their meaning
Use sine, cosine, tangent and Pythagoras in right triangles
Describe an AC quantity as a phasor
Convert between polar and rectangular form
explain: Most electrical calculations are the same few formulas rearranged. Keep the units with the numbers and the algebra stays safe.

AC voltages and currents rise and fall like sine waves. A phasor is an arrow: its length is the size of the quantity and its angle shows where it is in the cycle. Adding arrows is much easier than adding waves.
lessons.definition: A phasor represents a sinusoidal quantity by its magnitude and phase angle. Polar form: Z = r ∠ θ. Rectangular form: Z = a + jb, where j = √(−1) (engineers use j so it is not confused with current). r = √(a² + b²) and θ = tan⁻¹(b / a), taking care of the quadrant.

formulas.note: cosθ = adjacent / hypotenuse, tanθ = opposite / adjacent
Rectangular to polar

formulas.f: a = r cosθ   b = r sinθ
formulas.note: Polar to rectangular

example.question: (a) Convert 3 + j4 to polar form. (b) Convert 10 ∠ 30° to rectangular form.

applications: Impedance Z = R + jX is a phasor, and the impedance triangle is a right triangle.
The power triangle (P, Q, S) uses the same trigonometry.
Protection engineers read phasor diagrams of voltage and current to see the phase angle between them.
mistakes: Leaving the calculator in radians when the angle is in degrees (or the reverse).
Ignoring the quadrant: 3 − j4 and −3 + j4 have different angles.
Adding magnitudes of phasors instead of adding them as arrows.
lessons.safety: A calculation error in a protection or cable setting can leave equipment unprotected. Have important calculations checked by a second person.

quiz.q: A right triangle has sides 3 and 4. What is the hypotenuse?
What does j represent in electrical engineering?
quiz.why: j = √(−1); the letter i is kept for current.

quiz.q: What is cos 60°?

summary: Rearrange formulas carefully and keep units.
A phasor has magnitude and angle; convert with r = √(a²+b²) and a = r cosθ, b = r sinθ.
Check degrees versus radians on the calculator.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
objectives: Identify series and parallel connections
Calculate the total resistance of each
State what stays the same: current in series, voltage in parallel
explain: Series means one path: the same current passes through every component, like cars in a single lane. Parallel means several paths: the supply voltage is the same across each branch, like several lanes opening from the same road.
House sockets are in parallel so each gets the full supply voltage.
lessons.definition: In a series circuit the same current flows through every element and the voltages add up to the supply voltage. In a parallel circuit the same voltage appears across every branch and the branch currents add up to the total current.

formulas.note: Current is the same; the voltages add
Voltage is the same; the currents add

formulas.f: Two in parallel: R(total) = (R1 × R2) / (R1 + R2)
formulas.note: Shortcut for exactly two resistors

example.question: A 10 Ω and a 15 Ω resistor are connected to a 30 V supply, first in series and then in parallel. Find the total current each time.

applications: Contacts in a trip circuit are in series with the trip coil, so the coil energises only when the whole path is complete.
Lamps and sockets in a building are in parallel.
A short circuit is a very low-resistance path in parallel with the load, so the current becomes very large.
mistakes: Adding parallel resistances directly. The total is always smaller than the smallest branch.
Forgetting that voltage is the same across parallel branches.
Mixing up which quantity is shared in series and in parallel.
lessons.safety: A short circuit draws a very large current. That is why every circuit needs correctly rated fuses or breakers, and why you must never bridge terminals on a live supply.

quiz.q: Three 10 Ω resistors are in series. What is the total resistance?
quiz.why: Series resistances add: 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 Ω.

quiz.q: Two 20 Ω resistors are in parallel. What is the total resistance?
What is the same across every branch of a parallel circuit?
quiz.why: All branches are connected across the same two points, so they share the same voltage.

summary: Series: same current, resistances add.
Parallel: same voltage, 1/R adds, total is smaller than the smallest branch.
A short circuit is a very low-resistance parallel path.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
objectives: State Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) and voltage law (KVL)
Apply KCL at a junction
Apply KVL around a loop
Link KCL to differential protection
explain: KCL says charge cannot pile up at a junction: whatever current flows in must flow out. KVL says energy is conserved: going round a closed loop, the voltage rises from sources equal the voltage drops across components.
These two laws let you analyse circuits that are too complex for simple series and parallel rules.
lessons.definition: Kirchhoff's current law: the algebraic sum of the currents at any junction is zero, so the current entering equals the current leaving. Kirchhoff's voltage law: the algebraic sum of the voltages around any closed loop is zero.

formulas.note: Based on conservation of charge

formulas.f: KVL: Σ V = 0 around a closed loop
formulas.note: Based on conservation of energy

formulas.f: For a simple loop: E = I × R1 + I × R2 + …
formulas.note: Source voltage equals the sum of the drops

example.question: (a) A 12 V source is connected to 2 Ω and 4 Ω resistors in series. Find the current and each voltage drop, and check KVL. (b) At a junction 3 A and 2 A flow in and one wire carries current out. What is its current?

applications: Analysing circuits with several sources and loops.
Differential protection compares the current entering and leaving a protected zone. In a healthy zone these match, which is KCL applied to equipment, and a difference indicates an internal fault.
Checking CT and VT secondary wiring by following current paths and voltage drops.
mistakes: Using inconsistent sign conventions for current directions and voltage drops.
Applying KVL to a path that is not a closed loop.
Forgetting a branch current when applying KCL.
lessons.safety: When tracing a circuit on site, treat every conductor as energised until it has been isolated, proven dead and locked off according to your site procedure.

quiz.q: 4 A and 6 A flow into a junction and one other wire leaves it. What is the current in that wire?
quiz.why: KCL: current out = 4 + 6 = 10 A.

quiz.q: Kirchhoff's voltage law is based on conservation of what?
quiz.why: Going round a closed loop, energy gained equals energy lost.

quiz.q: The algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop equals what?
quiz.why: KVL: Σ V = 0 around any closed loop.

summary: KCL: current in = current out at a junction.
KVL: voltages around a closed loop sum to zero.
Differential protection is KCL applied to equipment.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Network Theorems: Superposition, Thevenin and Norton
objectives: Apply superposition to circuits with several sources
Find a Thevenin equivalent
Convert a Thevenin equivalent to a Norton equivalent
State the maximum power transfer condition
explain: Real circuits can be large, but from the point of view of one load they often behave like one simple source with one resistance in series. Thevenin and Norton find that simple version.
Superposition handles several sources by taking one source at a time and adding the results. It works only for linear circuits.
lessons.definition: Superposition: in a linear circuit the response is the sum of the responses to each source acting alone, with the other voltage sources replaced by short circuits and the other current sources by open circuits. Thevenin: a linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a voltage source Vth in series with a resistance Rth. Norton: the same network can be replaced by a current source In in parallel with Rn.

formulas.f: Vth = open-circuit voltage at the terminals
formulas.note: Remove the load first

formulas.f: Rth = resistance seen from the terminals with sources deactivated
formulas.note: Voltage sources become shorts; current sources become opens
Norton equivalent from Thevenin

formulas.f: Maximum power to a resistive load when RL = Rth
formulas.note: Then P(max) = Vth² / (4 × Rth)

example.question: A 12 V source feeds 6 Ω in series, then 3 Ω across the output terminals. Find the Thevenin and Norton equivalents seen at the terminals, then the current in a 2 Ω load connected there.
steps: Rth = 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω = (6 × 3) / 9 = 2 Ω
Load current I = Vth / (Rth + RL) = 4 / (2 + 2) = 1 A
example.answer: Vth = 4 V, Rth = 2 Ω; In = 2 A; load current 1 A

applications: Quickly recalculating load current when the load changes.
Power-system studies model the grid as a Thevenin source (voltage behind an impedance) when calculating fault current.
Matching a source to a load for maximum power in small signal circuits.
mistakes: Forgetting to remove the load before finding Vth.
Replacing sources the wrong way (voltage source to short, current source to open).
Using superposition on non-linear parts, or adding powers instead of currents or voltages.
lessons.safety: Replacing a source by a short circuit is only a step on paper. Never short-circuit a real live source.

quiz.q: When finding Rth, how is an ideal voltage source treated?
quiz.why: Voltage sources are replaced by shorts; current sources by opens.

quiz.q: Vth = 10 V and Rth = 5 Ω. What is the Norton current?
quiz.why: In = Vth / Rth = 10 / 5 = 2 A.

quiz.q: When is power transferred to a resistive load at its maximum?
quiz.why: Maximum power transfer occurs when the load resistance equals the Thevenin resistance.

summary: Superposition: one source at a time, then add (linear circuits only).
Thevenin: Vth in series with Rth. Norton: In = Vth / Rth in parallel with Rn = Rth.
Max power transfer when RL = Rth.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: AC Fundamentals, RMS and Phase
objectives: Describe a sinusoidal AC quantity
Calculate period, frequency and angular frequency
Convert between peak and RMS values
Explain phase difference, lead and lag
explain: Direct current flows one way. Alternating current reverses direction again and again, and the supply follows a sine wave. In India the grid frequency is 50 Hz, so there are 50 complete cycles every second.
A "230 V" supply is an RMS value. RMS is the DC value that would heat a resistor equally, so it is the number that matters for power.
lessons.definition: An alternating quantity such as v = Vm sin(ωt + φ) varies sinusoidally with time. Vm is the peak value, ω = 2πf is the angular frequency in rad/s, T = 1 / f is the period and φ is the phase angle. The RMS value of a sine wave is Vm / √2 ≈ 0.707 × Vm.

formulas.note: T in seconds, f in hertz (Hz), ω in rad/s
Applies to a pure sine wave only

formulas.f: Average of a half cycle = 2 × Vm / π ≈ 0.637 × Vm
formulas.note: Used for rectified waveforms

example.question: A 230 V (RMS) 50 Hz supply: find the peak voltage, period, angular frequency, and the voltage 5 ms after the start of a cycle (zero phase).
steps: v = 325.3 × sin(314.16 × 0.005) = 325.3 × sin(1.5708) = 325.3 V (the peak, at a quarter cycle)

applications: Meters and the supply rating use RMS values.
Directional relays compare the phase of voltage and current to decide the direction of a fault.
Insulation and test equipment must withstand the peak value, not just the RMS value.
mistakes: Using the peak value where the RMS value is needed.
Using 0.707 for waveforms that are not sine waves.
Mixing up lead and lag. If current lags voltage by 30°, then voltage leads current by 30°.
lessons.safety: The peak of a 230 V supply is about 325 V. Insulation, test leads and meters must be rated for the peak, and for the correct measurement category.

quiz.q: What is the RMS value of a sine wave with a 100 V peak?
What is the period of a 50 Hz supply?
Current lags voltage by 30°. What can you say?
quiz.why: If current lags, voltage leads by the same angle.

summary: Vrms = Vm / √2 for a sine wave; T = 1 / f; ω = 2πf.
RMS is the heating-equivalent value; supplies are quoted in RMS.
Phase difference decides lead or lag; protection relays use it.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Impedance, Resonance and Power Factor
objectives: Calculate reactance and impedance of series R, L and C circuits
Find the resonant frequency
Define power factor and its lagging or leading nature
Link impedance and power triangles
explain: In AC circuits, coils and capacitors oppose current without using energy on average. This opposition is reactance. Resistance and reactance combine as the sides of a right triangle to give impedance.
Power factor tells how much of the apparent power is doing real work. A low power factor means extra current for the same useful power.
lessons.definition: Inductive reactance XL = 2πfL and capacitive reactance XC = 1 / (2πfC), both in ohms. For a series RLC circuit the impedance is Z = √(R² + (XL − XC)²) and the phase angle is φ = tan⁻¹((XL − XC) / R). Power factor is cosφ. At series resonance XL = XC, the impedance is just R and the frequency is f0 = 1 / (2π√(LC)).

formulas.note: L in henry, C in farad
Series RLC circuit

formulas.f: pf = cosφ = R / Z = P / S
formulas.note: Inductive load: current lags (lagging pf)
Resonant frequency

example.question: A series circuit has R = 30 Ω and XL = 40 Ω (no capacitor) on 230 V. Find Z, current, power factor, P, Q and S. Then find the resonant frequency for L = 100 mH and C = 100 µF.

applications: Low power factor increases current, cable size and losses for the same kW, so capacitors are used to correct it.
Resonance is used in tuned filters and must be considered with capacitor banks and harmonics.
Motors and transformers are inductive, so they draw lagging current.
mistakes: Adding R and X directly. They add at right angles: Z = √(R² + X²).
Mixing up lagging and leading. An inductive load has lagging power factor.
Forgetting that XL rises with frequency while XC falls.
lessons.safety: Capacitors can stay charged after the supply is isolated. Discharge them and prove dead before touching. Resonance can cause very high currents and voltages.

quiz.q: R = 3 Ω and X = 4 Ω in series. What is Z?
R = 30 Ω and Z = 50 Ω. What is the power factor?
What is true at series resonance?
quiz.why: At resonance XL = XC, so the reactances cancel and Z = R.

summary: XL = 2πfL, XC = 1/(2πfC), Z = √(R² + X²).
pf = cosφ = R / Z = P / S; inductive loads are lagging.
Resonance at f0 = 1 / (2π√(LC)).

General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Single-Phase Circuits
objectives: Analyse series R-L and parallel R-L circuits on a single-phase supply
Find current, power factor and power
Add currents in parallel branches as phasors
explain: Most homes and small loads use a single-phase supply: one live (phase) conductor and one neutral. The load sees one sine wave of voltage.
In a series circuit the same current flows through every part, so impedances add as phasors. In a parallel circuit every branch sees the same voltage, so the branch currents add as phasors.
lessons.definition: In a series R-L circuit Z = √(R² + XL²), I = V / Z, the current lags the voltage by φ = tan⁻¹(XL / R) and the power factor is cosφ = R / Z. In a parallel R-L circuit each branch current is found from V, and the total current is the phasor sum: I = √(IR² + IL²), with the current lagging the voltage by tan⁻¹(IL / IR).

formulas.f: Series: Z = √(R² + XL²)   I = V / Z
formulas.note: pf = R / Z; P = I²R; Q = I²XL; S = V I

formulas.f: Parallel: IR = V / R   IL = V / XL
formulas.note: Branch currents

formulas.f: Parallel: I = √(IR² + IL²)   pf = IR / I
formulas.note: Currents add at right angles, not arithmetically

example.question: (a) A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a series circuit with R = 20 Ω and XL = 15 Ω. Find Z, I, pf, P, Q and S. (b) A resistor of 46 Ω is connected in parallel with an inductive reactance of 23 Ω on the same supply. Find the total current and the power factor.

applications: Domestic loads, lighting circuits and small motors run on single-phase supplies.
The same phasor method is used to analyse a relay coil, a CT burden or a motor winding.
Single-phase calculations are the building block for three-phase analysis, where each phase is treated like a single-phase circuit.
mistakes: Adding parallel branch currents arithmetically (5 + 10 = 15 A). They must be added as phasors.
Using R instead of Z to find the current in an AC circuit.
Forgetting that an inductive load gives a lagging power factor.
lessons.safety: The neutral conductor can be live under fault conditions, and a single-phase supply can still deliver a lethal shock. Isolate and prove dead before working, even on a "simple" circuit.

quiz.q: R = 20 Ω and XL = 15 Ω in series. What is Z?
IR = 5 A and IL = 10 A in parallel R-L branches. What is the total current?
quiz.why: I = √(5² + 10²) = 11.18 A, because the branch currents are 90° apart.

quiz.q: A series R-L circuit has R = 20 Ω and Z = 25 Ω. What is the power factor?

summary: Series: add impedances as phasors. Parallel: add branch currents as phasors.
pf = R / Z for series R-L; pf = IR / I for parallel R-L.
Inductive loads give lagging current.

practice.q: Series R = 30 Ω, XL = 40 Ω on 230 V. Find the current and power factor.
practice.a: Z = 50 Ω, I = 4.6 A, pf = 0.6 lagging

practice.q: Parallel R = 23 Ω and XL = 23 Ω on 230 V. Find the total current.

refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Three-Phase Systems
objectives: Describe a balanced three-phase supply
Relate line and phase quantities in star and delta
Calculate three-phase power
Explain why three-phase is used for power systems
explain: A three-phase supply has three voltages of the same size, each shifted by 120° from the next. Together they give a smooth flow of power, which suits large motors, transformers and generators.
Loads and sources can be connected in star (wye), with a common point, or in delta, in a closed triangle.
lessons.definition: In a balanced star connection the line voltage is √3 times the phase voltage and the line current equals the phase current. In a balanced delta connection the line voltage equals the phase voltage and the line current is √3 times the phase current. Total three-phase apparent power is S = √3 × VL × IL.

formulas.note: Line quantities are measured between lines / in the line
Phase quantities are those across / through each load phase

formulas.f: S = √3 VL IL   P = √3 VL IL cosφ   Q = √3 VL IL sinφ
formulas.note: VL, IL are line values; valid for balanced loads

example.question: A balanced load takes 100 A at power factor 0.8 lagging from a 415 V line supply. Find the phase voltage (star), S, P and Q.

applications: Generators, transmission lines, transformers and large motors are three-phase.
Three-phase supplies deliver the same power with less conductor material than single-phase.
Protection relays measure all three phases to detect phase and earth faults.
mistakes: Using phase voltage in S = √3 × VL × IL.
Assuming 415 V is the voltage of each phase to neutral.
Applying balanced-load formulas to a badly unbalanced load.
lessons.safety: Phase-to-phase voltage is higher than phase-to-neutral voltage, and a neutral can become live under fault conditions. Isolate, prove dead and lock off before working on any conductor.

quiz.q: A star supply has a 415 V line voltage. What is the phase voltage?
A delta load has a phase current of 10 A. What is the line current?
By how many degrees are balanced three-phase voltages displaced?
quiz.why: Each phase is displaced by 120° from the next.

summary: Star: VL = √3 Vph, IL = Iph. Delta: IL = √3 Iph, VL = Vph.
S = √3 VL IL; P = S cosφ.
Three-phase gives smooth power and uses less conductor material.
refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Star and Delta Connections
objectives: Convert between star and delta resistor networks
Compare line and phase currents for the same load
Explain why star-delta starting reduces starting current
explain: Three impedances can be joined in a Y shape (star) or in a closed triangle (delta). The same three impedances behave very differently on the same supply.
A star-delta starter starts a motor in star, with a lower voltage on each winding, and then switches it to delta for normal running.
lessons.definition: For balanced impedances, a delta network is equivalent to a star network with R(Y) = R(Δ) / 3. For the same line voltage and the same impedance per phase, a delta connection draws three times the line current and three times the power of a star connection. For three unequal delta resistors Rab, Rbc, Rca, the star resistor at node a is Ra = Rab × Rca / (Rab + Rbc + Rca).

formulas.note: Balanced networks
General delta to star (resistor at node a)
Same line voltage and same impedance per phase

example.question: (a) Three 12 Ω resistors are connected in delta. Find the equivalent star resistors. (b) A load of 12 Ω per phase is connected to a 415 V supply, first in star and then in delta. Compare the line currents.
steps: (b) Star: Vph = 415 / √3 = 239.6 V, I = 239.6 / 12 = 19.97 A (line current = phase current)
Delta: Iph = 415 / 12 = 34.58 A, line current = √3 × 34.58 = 59.9 A
example.answer: (a) 4 Ω each   (b) star 19.97 A, delta 59.9 A (three times)

applications: Star-delta starters reduce the starting current and torque to about one third of the direct-on-line values.
Motor terminal boxes allow the windings to be connected in star or delta, so the supply and nameplate voltage must match.
Transformer winding connections (for example Dyn11) use star and delta ideas.
mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 3 between star and delta equivalents.
Mixing up line and phase quantities.
Connecting a motor in delta when its nameplate says star for that supply voltage.
lessons.safety: Changing a star-delta connection changes the voltage across each winding. A wrong connection can overheat or burn out a motor. Isolate, check the nameplate and verify the connection diagram before energising.

quiz.q: Three 30 Ω resistors in delta. What is each equivalent star resistor?
Same load on the same supply: how does the delta line current compare with star?
quiz.why: Delta draws three times the line current of star.

quiz.q: Why is a motor started in star?
quiz.why: Star reduces the voltage across each winding, so the starting current is about one third.

summary: R(Y) = R(Δ) / 3 for balanced networks.
Delta draws 3 times the line current and power of star on the same supply.
Star-delta starting cuts starting current and torque to about one third.

practice.q: Delta resistors Rab = 10 Ω, Rbc = 20 Ω, Rca = 30 Ω. Find Ra.

refs: IEC 60050 (Electropedia) for the terms
Motor nameplate and the manufacturer's connection diagram for the actual winding connection

lessons.title: Active, Reactive and Apparent Power
objectives: Define P, Q and S and their units
Use the power triangle
Calculate P, Q and S from V, I and power factor
explain: Not all the current drawn by an AC load does useful work. Think of a glass of beer: the liquid is the useful power (P), the foam is the reactive power (Q), and the whole glass is the apparent power (S).
Reactive power moves back and forth between the source and the magnetic or electric fields of the load. It does no net work, but it still loads the cables and transformers.
lessons.definition: Active (real) power P is the average power that does useful work, in watts (W). Reactive power Q is the power exchanged with magnetic and electric fields, in volt-ampere reactive (var). Apparent power S = V × I, in volt-amperes (VA). They form a right triangle: S² = P² + Q², with P = S cosφ and Q = S sinφ.

formulas.f: S = V × I   (three-phase: S = √3 × VL × IL)
formulas.note: S in VA (or kVA)

formulas.f: P = S cosφ = V I cosφ
formulas.note: P in W (or kW)

formulas.f: Q = S sinφ = V I sinφ
formulas.note: Q in var (or kvar); positive for an inductive (lagging) load
Power triangle

example.question: A single-phase load takes 10 A from a 230 V supply at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. Find S, P and Q.

applications: Transformers and generators are rated in kVA because their heating depends on voltage and current, not on the power factor.
Energy meters record active energy (kWh); some also record reactive energy (kvarh).
Protection and control systems measure P and Q to supervise power flow.
mistakes: Adding kW and kVA directly. They are different quantities.
Using S = P + Q. The correct relation is S² = P² + Q².
Mixing up the sign of Q for lagging and leading loads.
lessons.safety: Equipment must be sized for the apparent power (the current it carries), not just the kW. Check kVA and current ratings on the nameplate before connecting a load.

quiz.q: P = 3 kW and Q = 4 kvar. What is S?
What is the unit of reactive power?
quiz.why: Reactive power is measured in var (volt-ampere reactive).

quiz.q: Why are transformers rated in kVA?
options: Because they only carry reactive power
Because heating depends on voltage and current
Because kW is not an SI unit
Because their power factor is always 1
quiz.why: Losses and heating depend on the current and voltage, whatever the load power factor.

summary: S = VI; P = S cosφ; Q = S sinφ; S² = P² + Q².
Units: VA, W, var.
Size equipment for kVA, not only kW.

practice.q: A load has P = 5 kW at pf 0.9 lagging. Find S and Q.

refs: IEC 60050 (International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, Electropedia) for definitions
General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Power Factor and Correction
objectives: Explain why a low power factor is a problem
Calculate the capacitor kvar needed for correction
Describe the risks of over-correction
explain: Most industrial loads, such as motors and transformers, are inductive. They draw lagging reactive current, so the supply carries more current than the useful kW needs.
A capacitor supplies reactive power locally, so the supply does not have to. The current falls, even though the useful power stays the same.
lessons.definition: Power factor correction adds capacitive reactive power to reduce the lagging reactive power drawn from the supply. To raise the power factor from cosφ1 to cosφ2 for an active load P, the capacitor rating needed is Qc = P × (tanφ1 − tanφ2).

formulas.note: Qc in kvar when P is in kW
Line current of a balanced three-phase load
Power factor

example.question: A 100 kW three-phase load at 415 V has a power factor of 0.8 lagging. Find the capacitor kvar to raise it to 0.95, and the line current before and after.
example.answer: About 42.1 kvar; line current falls from 173.9 A to 146.4 A

applications: Automatic power factor correction (APFC) panels switch capacitor steps to follow the load.
Lower current means lower cable and transformer losses and more spare capacity.
Some utilities apply tariff conditions based on power factor. Check your own supplier's rules.
mistakes: Using kVA instead of kW as P in the formula.
Over-correcting, which gives a leading power factor and can raise the voltage.
Ignoring harmonics. Capacitors can resonate with the network, so detuned reactors may be needed.
lessons.safety: Capacitor banks keep stored charge after isolation. Wait for the discharge time given by the manufacturer, then prove dead and short the terminals as per the site procedure before touching.

quiz.q: What unit is used for the rating of a capacitor bank?
quiz.why: Capacitors supply reactive power, measured in kvar.

quiz.q: After correction, what happens to the line current for the same kW load?
quiz.why: I = P / (√3 × VL × pf), so a higher pf gives a lower current.

quiz.q: Which load is typically lagging?
quiz.why: Motors are inductive, so their current lags the voltage.

summary: Qc = P (tanφ1 − tanφ2).
Higher pf means lower current for the same kW.
Avoid over-correction and check harmonics.

practice.q: A 50 kW load at pf 0.7 lagging is corrected to 0.95. Find Qc.

refs: IEC 60050 (Electropedia) for the terms
Your electricity supplier's published tariff conditions, for any penalty or incentive rules

lessons.title: Basic Electrical Measurements
lessons.prereq: Voltage, EMF and Potential Difference; Electric Charge and Current
objectives: Measure voltage, current, resistance and continuity correctly
Explain how a clamp meter works in principle
Estimate the uncertainty of a digital meter reading
Choose a meter with the right category rating
explain: A multimeter measures voltage across two points. Current is measured by putting the meter in the path of the current (or by using a clamp). Resistance is measured with the circuit dead.
A clamp meter senses the magnetic field around a conductor, so it can read current without breaking the circuit.
lessons.definition: A digital multimeter reading has an uncertainty given by the manufacturer, for example ±(x % of reading + n digits). Voltage is measured with the meter in parallel; current with the meter in series, or with a clamp around one conductor; resistance and continuity only on a de-energised circuit. The measurement category (CAT I to IV, IEC 61010) shows the transient overvoltage the meter is designed for.

formulas.note: High input resistance, so it draws almost no current

formulas.f: Current: meter in series (or a clamp on one conductor)
formulas.note: A series meter has very low resistance

formulas.f: Uncertainty = ±(% of reading × reading + digits × resolution)
formulas.note: Use your own meter's datasheet values

example.question: A meter reads 230.0 V (resolution 0.1 V). Its datasheet says ±(0.5 % of reading + 2 digits). What is the possible range of the true value?

applications: Electricians check supply voltage with a multimeter before and after work.
Clamp meters measure load current without opening a circuit.
Continuity checks confirm wiring before energising.
mistakes: Putting the leads in the current (A) jack and then measuring voltage. This forms a near short circuit.
Measuring resistance on a live circuit.
Clamping a meter around both the live and neutral conductors together. The currents cancel and the reading is close to zero.
lessons.safety: Use a meter whose category and voltage rating suit the installation, with undamaged leads and fuses. Check the lead positions and the selected mode before every measurement. Never measure resistance on an energised circuit, and follow your site isolation procedure.

quiz.q: How is a voltmeter connected to a component?
quiz.why: A voltmeter measures the voltage across two points.

quiz.q: Resistance should be measured on a circuit that is…
quiz.why: The meter injects its own small current, so the circuit must be dead.

quiz.q: A clamp meter is placed around both conductors of a single-phase cable. The reading is…
quiz.why: The currents in the two conductors are equal and opposite, so their magnetic fields cancel.

summary: Voltage in parallel, current in series (or clamp), resistance when dead.
Uncertainty = ± (% of reading + digits).
Use the correct CAT-rated meter and check the lead jacks.

practice.q: A meter reads 12.00 V with spec ±(0.5 % + 3 digits), resolution 0.01 V. Find the uncertainty.

refs: IEC 61010-1 (safety requirements for electrical equipment for measurement, control and laboratory use)
The meter manufacturer's datasheet for accuracy and category rating

lessons.title: Electrical Safety Fundamentals
objectives: Explain the main electrical hazards
Describe safe isolation: isolate, lock off, prove dead
Explain why working practices and permits exist
Know where to find the legal and standard requirements
explain: Electricity cannot be seen, heard or smelled until it hurts. The main hazards are electric shock, burns and arcs, and fire. Even small currents through the body can be dangerous, and the effect depends on the current, the path and how long it flows.
Safe work is built on layers: remove the hazard first (isolate), then control what remains (earthing, barriers, PPE, trained people, permits).
lessons.definition: Safe isolation is a controlled sequence that makes equipment dead and keeps it dead while work is done: identify the sources, isolate, lock and tag, test the tester, test the circuit, test the tester again (prove-test-prove), and earth where required, all under the approved permit or procedure.

formulas.f: Hazards: shock, arc flash and burns, fire
formulas.note: Voltage, available fault energy and the person's contact path all matter

formulas.f: Isolate → Lock and tag → Prove dead
formulas.note: The core of safe isolation

formulas.f: Always: assume live until proven dead
formulas.note: Applies to every conductor and terminal

example.question: Describe the safe isolation sequence for a motor feeder before maintenance.
steps: 1. Identify every source that can energise the motor and its control circuit.
2. Switch off and isolate each source; fit your personal lock and tag.
3. Check a voltage tester on a known live source or proving unit.
4. Test every conductor of the motor circuit with that tester and confirm it is dead.
5. Re-check the tester on the known source.
6. Apply earthing if required and work under the permit or approved procedure.
example.answer: Isolate, lock and tag, then test–prove–test, then work under permit

applications: Maintenance on motor starters, panels and feeders uses lockout and tagout.
Substation work uses permits to work and authorised persons.
RCDs and earthing limit shock risk, but they do not replace safe working.
mistakes: Assuming a circuit is dead because a switch is off.
Working alone, or without the right permit.
Using damaged leads or an unrated tester.
lessons.safety: Never work on energised equipment unless the task is authorised, trained for and done with approved procedures and equipment. This course does not replace training, site rules, permits or supervision.

quiz.q: What should you assume about an electrical conductor before testing it?
options: It is live until proven dead
quiz.why: Treat every conductor as live until you have proved it dead.

quiz.q: What does "prove-test-prove" mean?
options: Test the tester on a known source, test the circuit, then test the tester again
quiz.why: It confirms the tester worked before and after the dead test.

quiz.q: Which comes first in safe working?
quiz.why: Eliminating the hazard by isolation is better than relying on PPE.

summary: Hazards: shock, arc flash and burns, fire.
Isolate, lock and tag, prove dead (test-prove-test).
Follow permits, procedures and training.

practice.q: Why must the voltage tester be checked on a known live source before and after the test?
practice.a: So that a faulty tester cannot wrongly show that a live circuit is dead.

refs: Electricity Act, 2003 (India)
Central Electricity Authority (CEA) safety regulations: confirm the current notified version on the CEA website
Your employer's or site's approved safety rules and permit procedures

lessons.title: Worked Numerical Problems: Fundamentals
objectives: Combine several formulas in one problem
Set out a calculation clearly with units
Check an answer for sense
explain: Real problems mix several ideas. A reliable method is: write what is given, choose the formula, convert units, calculate, then check that the answer is sensible.
These problems revisit cable resistance, energy, parallel circuits, three-phase motors and transformers.
lessons.definition: A worked problem is solved by listing the given values with units, choosing the correct formulas, substituting values in consistent SI units, and checking the magnitude and units of the result.

formulas.note: Three-phase motor input current; P(input) = P(output) / efficiency
Single-phase cable, out and back

formulas.f: E = P × t   Vs = Vp × Ns / Np
formulas.note: Energy and ideal transformer ratio

example.question: A three-phase induction motor delivers 11 kW at its shaft. Its efficiency is 0.9 and its power factor is 0.85 lagging, on a 415 V supply. Find the line current.

applications: Estimating the current of a motor before choosing a cable and protection.
Checking voltage drop and energy cost.
Quick sense checks on test and commissioning readings.
mistakes: Forgetting efficiency, so the input power is taken as the output power.
Mixing kW and W, or mm² and m².
Not checking whether the answer is reasonable.
lessons.safety: Calculated currents are for learning. Real cable and protection selection must follow the applicable standard, the manufacturer data and a qualified engineer.

quiz.q: A motor delivers 11 kW at 0.9 efficiency. What is its input power?
quiz.why: Input = output / efficiency = 11 / 0.9 = 12.2 kW.

quiz.q: 12 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel across 24 V. What is the total current?
The peak of an 11 kV (RMS) sine wave is about…

summary: Write given values, formula, units, calculate, check.
Use efficiency to go from output to input power.
Convert to SI units before calculating.

practice.q: A 40 A single-phase load is 50 m from the supply (one way) on 6 mm² copper (ρ = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m). Find the voltage drop and its percentage of 230 V (ignore reactance).
A 1.5 kW heater runs 4 hours a day for 30 days. Find the energy, and the cost at an assumed ₹6 per kWh.
Find the secondary turns of an ideal 11 kV / 415 V transformer with 1000 primary turns.

General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Resistors, Inductors and Capacitors in Practice
objectives: Read a resistor colour code
Choose a resistor power rating
Understand capacitor voltage rating and polarity
Know the main inductor ratings
explain: Real components have ratings, not just values. A 100 Ω resistor must also be able to survive the heat, and a capacitor must be able to withstand the voltage across it.
Always read three things on any component: its value, its tolerance and its rating (power, voltage or current).
lessons.definition: Resistors are specified by resistance, tolerance and power rating (P = I²R). Preferred values follow E-series (for example E12 and E24). Capacitors are specified by capacitance, tolerance and rated voltage; electrolytic capacitors are polarised and have equivalent series resistance (ESR). Inductors are specified by inductance and rated current, and the core can saturate if the rated current is exceeded.

formulas.note: Black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, grey 8, white 9; gold ±5 %, silver ±10 %, brown ±1 %
Power dissipated in a resistor; the rating should be well above this

formulas.f: Capacitor voltage rating > peak working voltage
formulas.note: For 230 V AC the peak is about 325 V

example.question: (a) A resistor is banded brown, black, red, gold. Find its value and tolerance. (b) A 100 Ω resistor carries 0.2 A. Find the power dissipated and suggest a rating. (c) A capacitor is used across a 230 V AC supply. What minimum voltage rating does the peak voltage suggest?
steps: (a) Brown = 1, black = 0, red = × 10², so 10 × 100 = 1000 Ω = 1 kΩ; gold = ±5 %
(b) P = 0.2² × 100 = 4 W. A common practice is to choose a rating at least twice the dissipation, so a 10 W resistor
(c) Peak = √2 × 230 = 325 V, so the rating must be above 325 V, and a higher rating gives margin per the manufacturer data
example.answer: (a) 1 kΩ ±5 %   (b) 4 W, use about 10 W   (c) above 325 V

applications: Resistors limit current and set bias in electronic circuits and in protection relay inputs.
Capacitors smooth supplies, start single-phase motors and correct power factor.
Inductors filter, store energy and limit current in power circuits.
mistakes: Ignoring the power rating, so the resistor overheats.
Reading the colour code from the wrong end.
Connecting a polarised electrolytic capacitor the wrong way round.
lessons.safety: An electrolytic capacitor connected in reverse or over its voltage rating can fail violently. Charged capacitors can shock after isolation, so discharge them. High-power resistors become very hot.

quiz.q: Orange, orange, brown, gold. What is the value?
A 100 Ω resistor carries 0.5 A. What power does it dissipate?
Which capacitor type is polarised?
quiz.why: Electrolytic capacitors must be connected with the correct polarity.

summary: Check value, tolerance and rating.
P = I²R and choose a rating with margin.
Respect capacitor polarity and voltage rating.

practice.q: Red, red, orange, silver. Find the value and tolerance.
A 47 Ω resistor carries 0.1 A. Find the power.

General reading: B. L. Theraja, A Textbook of Electrical Technology, Volume I

lessons.title: Diodes, Transistors and Basic Electronic Components
objectives: Explain how a diode conducts and what a rectifier does
Size a series resistor for an LED
Describe the BJT, MOSFET, IGBT and thyristor roles
Estimate the DC peak from a bridge rectifier
explain: A diode is a one-way valve for current. It conducts when forward-biased and blocks when reverse-biased, which is how AC is turned into DC.
A transistor is an electronic switch or amplifier. A small control signal decides whether a much larger current flows. Power devices such as IGBTs do this in inverters and drives.
lessons.definition: A silicon diode conducts when forward-biased with a drop of about 0.7 V. A Zener diode is operated in reverse breakdown to hold a roughly constant voltage; an LED needs a series resistor to limit its current. In a BJT the collector current is Ic = β × Ib in the active region. MOSFETs and IGBTs are voltage-controlled devices used in power electronics, and a thyristor (SCR) latches on after a gate pulse.

formulas.note: Series resistor for an LED; Vf from the datasheet (about 2 V is typical, depending on colour)
Bridge rectifier output peak, with two diodes conducting at a time
Transistor in the active region

example.question: (a) An LED has Vf = 2 V and is run at 10 mA from 12 V. Find the series resistor and its power. (b) A bridge rectifier is fed from 12 V RMS. Estimate the DC peak with 0.7 V drops. (c) A BJT with β = 100 has Ib = 0.1 mA. Find Ic.

applications: Rectifiers and DC power supplies in control panels and chargers.
IGBTs and MOSFETs switch the power in VFDs, inverters and UPS systems.
LEDs and Zener diodes are used for indication and simple voltage references in relay and control circuits.
mistakes: Connecting an LED without a series resistor.
Ignoring the diode forward drop in rectifier calculations.
Applying the transistor formula Ic = βIb when the device is saturated.
lessons.safety: Power semiconductors and their heat sinks can be very hot, and DC bus capacitors in drives hold dangerous charge after isolation. Wait for the discharge time and prove dead before working.

quiz.q: What is the approximate forward drop of a silicon diode?
quiz.why: About 0.7 V for silicon.

quiz.q: Which device is commonly used to switch power in inverters and drives?
quiz.why: IGBTs and MOSFETs are the main power switches in drives.

quiz.q: A BJT has β = 50 and Ib = 0.2 mA. What is Ic?

summary: A diode conducts one way, with about 0.7 V drop for silicon.
LEDs need a series resistor R = (Vs − Vf) / I.
IGBTs and MOSFETs are the power switches of modern drives.

practice.q: An LED (Vf = 2 V) runs at 20 mA from 5 V. Find R.
A bridge fed from 24 V RMS: estimate the DC peak with 0.7 V drops.
