lessons.title: Fuses
lessons.prereq: Power and Energy; Basic Electrical Measurements
objectives: Explain how a fuse works and why it is a sacrificial device
Describe HRC fuse construction and common fuse types
Use rated current, voltage and breaking capacity
Apply the basic rule: load current ≤ fuse rating ≤ cable rating
explain: A fuse is the weak link in a circuit on purpose. If too much current flows, the fuse element heats up and melts, opening the circuit before the cable or equipment is damaged.
The sand-filled body of an HRC fuse cools and quenches the arc that forms when the element melts, so even a very large fault current can be interrupted safely.
lessons.definition: A fuse is an overcurrent protective device with a calibrated element that melts and opens the circuit when the current and time exceed its characteristic. Key ratings are the rated current In, rated voltage, breaking capacity (the highest prospective fault current it can safely interrupt), the time-current characteristic and the let-through energy I²t. Under IEC 60269, gG fuses are general-purpose (full-range) and aM fuses are partial-range, intended for motor circuits.

formulas.note: Design current ≤ fuse rating ≤ current-carrying capacity of the cable
The fuse must let through less energy than the cable can withstand; k is a material constant, S the conductor area in mm²
At the point where the fuse is installed

example.question: (a) A circuit has a design current of 12 A and a cable whose current-carrying capacity is 20 A. Which standard fuse rating would you choose? (b) A 2.5 mm² copper PVC cable has k = 115. Is it protected by a fuse with a let-through energy of 20 000 A²s?
steps: (a) Need 12 A ≤ In ≤ 20 A; the preferred rating 16 A satisfies this
20 000 A²s is less than 82 656 A²s, so the cable withstands the fuse let-through energy
example.answer: (a) 16 A   (b) Yes, on this check alone (also check the overload rule and the applicable wiring standard)

applications: HRC fuses protect motor starters, switchgear, panels and cables in industrial installations.
Fuses give fast current limiting on high fault currents.
Small cartridge and blade fuses protect electronic and vehicle circuits.
mistakes: Replacing a fuse with a higher rating, or bridging it with wire.
Choosing a fuse by current rating only and ignoring breaking capacity.
Fitting a different type or voltage class of fuse than the one specified.
lessons.safety: Isolate before removing a fuse and use the correct fuse puller or handle. Always replace a blown fuse with one of the same type, rating and voltage class, and find out why it blew before re-energising.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of the sand in an HRC fuse?
options: To cool and quench the arc
quiz.why: The filler absorbs heat and extinguishes the arc.

quiz.q: A circuit carries 12 A and the cable can carry 20 A. Which rating satisfies Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz?
quiz.why: 16 A lies between 12 A and 20 A.

quiz.q: What must a fuse's breaking capacity be at least equal to?
options: The prospective short-circuit current at its location
quiz.why: Otherwise the fuse may not safely interrupt a fault.

summary: A fuse melts to open the circuit and is replaced after operating.
Choose Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz and check breaking capacity and I²t.
Never replace with a different type or bridge the fuse.

practice.q: A cable has k = 115 and S = 4 mm². Find k²S².

refs: IEC 60269 series (low-voltage fuses): confirm the current edition and the part for your fuse type
IEC 60364-4-43 (protection against overcurrent) for the Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz rule: confirm against the wiring rules that apply in your country

lessons.title: Circuit Breakers: MCB, MCCB, ACB and VCB
objectives: Explain what a circuit breaker does and how it differs from a fuse
Compare MCB, MCCB, ACB and VCB by application
Interpret trip curves B, C and D
Explain rated current and breaking capacity
explain: A circuit breaker is an automatic switch. Unlike a fuse it can be reset after it trips. It opens when the current is too high for too long (overload) or very high (short circuit).
The four types cover different sizes: MCBs for final circuits, MCCBs for feeders and panels, ACBs for large low-voltage incomers, and VCBs for medium-voltage systems.
lessons.definition: A circuit breaker is a mechanical switching device able to make, carry and break normal and fault currents. An MCB (miniature circuit breaker, IEC 60898-1) is used for final circuits and has type B, C and D magnetic trip ranges of 3 to 5, 5 to 10 and 10 to 20 times In. An MCCB (moulded-case) and an ACB (air circuit breaker) are low-voltage industrial breakers covered by IEC 60947-2, often with adjustable trip units. A VCB (vacuum circuit breaker) interrupts the arc inside a vacuum interrupter in medium-voltage equipment (IEC 62271-100).

formulas.f: Type B: 3 to 5 × In   Type C: 5 to 10 × In   Type D: 10 to 20 × In
formulas.note: Instantaneous (magnetic) trip range of an MCB
Icn for MCBs; Icu and Ics for IEC 60947-2 breakers

formulas.f: Ics is often declared as a percentage of Icu
formulas.note: Service breaking capacity compared with ultimate breaking capacity

example.question: (a) A 16 A MCB is available in types B, C and D. Find the range of current at which the instantaneous trip operates for each. (b) The prospective short-circuit current at the installation point is 6 kA. What must be true of the breaker's breaking capacity?
steps: (b) The rated breaking capacity must be at least 6 kA (for example a 10 kA rated device)
example.answer: (a) B: 48 to 80 A, C: 80 to 160 A, D: 160 to 320 A   (b) Breaking capacity of 6 kA or more

applications: MCBs protect lighting and socket circuits; type C and D suit loads with high inrush such as motors and transformers.
MCCBs protect feeders and motor circuits in distribution boards and panels.
ACBs are used as main incomers in low-voltage switchboards, and VCBs in 11 kV and similar medium-voltage switchgear.
mistakes: Choosing a breaker by current rating alone and ignoring the breaking capacity.
Assuming a breaker can always be used as an isolator. Only breakers marked for isolation can.
Using a type B breaker on a load with high inrush current, which causes nuisance tripping.
lessons.safety: A breaker that is open is not always proven dead. Isolate, lock off and test. ACB and VCB mechanisms store spring energy, and racking breakers in or out must be done only by trained persons using the approved procedure, with arc-flash precautions.

quiz.q: Which MCB type has an instantaneous trip range of 5 to 10 times In?
quiz.why: Type C trips instantaneously at 5 to 10 × In.

quiz.q: Where is a VCB normally used?
quiz.why: Vacuum circuit breakers are used in medium-voltage equipment.

quiz.q: Prospective short-circuit current is 6 kA. A breaker with a breaking capacity of 3 kA is…
options: Acceptable if it is type D
quiz.why: The breaking capacity must be at least the prospective fault current.

summary: MCB, MCCB, ACB: low voltage; VCB: medium voltage.
MCB types: B 3 to 5, C 5 to 10, D 10 to 20 × In.
Select by rated current, breaking capacity and trip characteristic.

practice.q: Find the instantaneous trip range of a 32 A type C MCB.

refs: IEC 60898-1 (circuit-breakers for household and similar installations)
IEC 60947-2 (low-voltage circuit-breakers)
IEC 62271-100 (high-voltage alternating-current circuit-breakers)
Manufacturer datasheets for the actual ratings: confirm the current edition of each standard

lessons.title: RCCB and RCBO
objectives: Explain how a residual current device detects earth leakage
Distinguish RCCB from RCBO
Interpret the rated residual current IΔn
Know what an RCD does not protect against
explain: In a healthy circuit the current going out on the live conductor equals the current coming back on the neutral. If some current leaks to earth, perhaps through a person, the two no longer match.
An RCD senses that difference, called the residual current, and trips quickly. This is Kirchhoff's current law used as a safety device.
lessons.definition: A residual current device (RCD) measures the vector sum of the line and neutral currents with a core-balance current transformer and trips when the residual current exceeds its rated residual operating current IΔn. An RCCB is a residual-current operated circuit-breaker without overcurrent protection (IEC 61008-1) and must be backed by a fuse or MCB. An RCBO adds integral overcurrent protection (IEC 61009-1). Types AC, A, F and B differ in the residual waveforms they can detect.

formulas.note: Zero in a healthy single-phase circuit

formulas.f: Trips for residual current up to IΔn; must not trip at 0.5 × IΔn
formulas.note: Typical IEC behaviour of a general-type RCD

formulas.f: Common IΔn ratings: 30 mA (personal protection), 100 mA, 300 mA
formulas.note: Choose according to the application and local rules

example.question: A 30 mA RCD protects a circuit. The live current is 10.00 A and the neutral return current is 9.98 A. What is the residual current, and will the RCD trip?
steps: The RCD must not trip below 0.5 × 30 = 15 mA and must trip at 30 mA
20 mA lies between 15 mA and 30 mA, so the RCD may or may not trip
example.answer: 20 mA: in the band where tripping is allowed but not guaranteed

applications: 30 mA RCDs add protection against shock in sockets and wet areas.
Higher-rated RCDs (such as 300 mA) are used mainly for fire protection and in distribution circuits.
Special RCD types are needed where DC or non-sinusoidal leakage currents are present, for example some EV charging and inverter circuits.
mistakes: Thinking an RCCB gives overload or short-circuit protection. It does not; it needs an MCB or fuse.
Assuming an RCD protects against touching live and neutral together. The currents are balanced, so it does not trip.
Sharing a neutral between two RCD-protected circuits, which causes nuisance tripping.
lessons.safety: An RCD is an additional protection, not a replacement for good earthing, insulation and safe working. Use the test button periodically as the manufacturer advises, and still isolate and prove dead before working on any circuit.

quiz.q: What does an RCD measure?
quiz.why: It compares the live and neutral currents.

quiz.q: Which device combines residual-current and overcurrent protection?
quiz.why: RCBO has integral overcurrent protection.

quiz.q: A 30 mA RCD must not trip at what residual current?
quiz.why: A general-type RCD must not trip at half its rated residual current.

summary: Residual current = live current − neutral current.
RCCB: leakage only. RCBO: leakage plus overcurrent.
30 mA RCDs give additional protection against shock.

practice.q: Live current is 5.00 A and neutral return is 4.95 A. Find the residual current.
practice.a: 0.05 A = 50 mA, which exceeds 30 mA, so a 30 mA RCD must trip

refs: IEC 61008-1 (RCCBs)
IEC 61009-1 (RCBOs)
Your local wiring regulations for where RCDs are required: confirm the current edition

lessons.title: Contactors and Auxiliary Relays
lessons.prereq: Circuit Breakers; Series and Parallel Circuits
objectives: Explain how a contactor and a relay work
Distinguish main contacts from auxiliary contacts (NO and NC)
Understand utilization categories AC-1, AC-3 and AC-4
Explain why a contactor is not a protective device
explain: A contactor is an electrically operated switch for power circuits. A small current in the coil creates a magnetic pull that closes the main contacts, so a push button or PLC output can switch a large motor.
An auxiliary relay works the same way on a smaller scale. It gives extra contacts or repeats a signal, so one control signal can operate several circuits.
lessons.definition: A contactor is a mechanical switching device with a single rest position, operated other than by hand, able to make, carry and break normal load currents, including overload conditions (IEC 60947-4-1). Its main contacts carry the load; auxiliary contacts (normally open NO or normally closed NC) are used in control circuits. Utilization categories describe the duty: AC-1 for non-inductive or slightly inductive loads, AC-3 for starting and switching off squirrel-cage motors while running, and AC-4 for plugging and inching. Control relays follow IEC 61810-1.

formulas.note: Full-load current of a three-phase motor

formulas.f: I(coil) = V / R(coil)   P(coil) = V × I
formulas.note: Coil current and power for a DC coil

formulas.f: Contactor AC-3 rating ≥ motor full-load current
formulas.note: Then check starting duty and the manufacturer coordination tables

example.question: (a) A 7.5 kW three-phase motor has an efficiency of 0.88 and power factor 0.85 on 415 V. Find its full-load current to help choose a contactor. (b) A 24 V DC relay coil has a resistance of 1.2 kΩ. Find the coil current and power.
steps: Choose a contactor with an AC-3 rating above 13.9 A and check the manufacturer data

applications: Direct-on-line and star-delta motor starters use contactors with an overload relay and short-circuit protection.
Auxiliary relays repeat signals, add contacts and interface PLC outputs with higher-voltage circuits.
Protection relay outputs often drive contactors or breaker coils through auxiliary contacts.
mistakes: Choosing a contactor by its AC-1 current rating for a motor. Use the AC-3 rating.
Assuming a contactor protects against overload or short circuit. It needs an overload relay and fuses or a breaker.
Leaving a DC coil without suppression, which can damage the driving contact or transistor.
lessons.safety: Contact tips can weld, so a contactor is not proof of isolation. Isolate upstream, lock off and prove dead. Never press the armature by hand on live equipment, because the contacts close.

quiz.q: Which utilization category is used for starting and running squirrel-cage motors?
quiz.why: AC-3 covers squirrel-cage motors starting and switching off while running.

quiz.q: A 24 V DC coil has a resistance of 1.2 kΩ. What is the coil current?
A contactor alone provides…
quiz.why: A contactor switches the load. Protection comes from separate devices.

summary: A coil operates the main contacts; auxiliary contacts serve the control circuit.
Use the AC-3 rating for motors.
A contactor switches; it does not protect or isolate.

practice.q: A 5.5 kW motor, efficiency 0.85, pf 0.85, 415 V. Find the full-load current.

refs: IEC 60947-4-1 (contactors and motor-starters, electromechanical)
IEC 61810-1 (electromechanical elementary relays)
Manufacturer datasheets for ratings and coordination: confirm the current editions

lessons.title: Isolators and Disconnectors
objectives: Explain the purpose of an isolator or disconnector
Distinguish isolators from circuit breakers and switch-disconnectors
State the correct operating sequence with a breaker
Explain the role of earthing switches and interlocks
explain: A circuit breaker interrupts current. An isolator does a different job: it creates a safe, visible or reliably indicated gap so that work can be done on the other side.
Think of the breaker as the tap that stops the water and the isolator as the lock on the valve that proves nobody can turn it back on.
lessons.definition: An isolator (disconnector) is a mechanical switching device that provides, in the open position, an isolating distance that meets specified safety requirements. A disconnector is normally operated off load and is not intended to break load current. A switch-disconnector can make and break load current and also provides isolation (IEC 60947-3 for low voltage; IEC 62271-102 for high-voltage disconnectors and earthing switches). An earthing switch connects isolated equipment to earth for safety.

formulas.f: Operate isolators only with the breaker open
formulas.note: The breaker breaks the current; the isolator isolates

formulas.f: De-energise: breaker open → isolators open → earth switch closed
formulas.note: Re-energise in the reverse order

formulas.f: Switch-disconnector ratings use categories such as AC-21, AC-22 and AC-23
formulas.note: Resistive, mixed and motor loads respectively

example.question: Describe the correct sequence to take a feeder out of service for work and put it back.
steps: Take out of service: 1. Open the circuit breaker. 2. Open the line and busbar isolators and confirm the open position. 3. Prove dead with an approved tester. 4. Close the earthing switch. 5. Lock, tag and work under permit.
Return to service: 1. Confirm work is complete and the permit is cancelled. 2. Open the earthing switch. 3. Close the isolators with the breaker still open. 4. Close the circuit breaker.
example.answer: Breaker first and last; isolators only with the breaker open; earth the isolated section

applications: Substations use isolators on both sides of a breaker so it can be isolated for maintenance.
Panels use switch-disconnectors as the main on-load switch for each section.
Interlocks, mechanical or electrical, stop an isolator being operated while the breaker is closed.
mistakes: Opening an isolator while load current is flowing, which can cause a dangerous arc.
Treating an open breaker as proof that the circuit is isolated.
Bypassing or forcing an interlock.
lessons.safety: Never operate a disconnector on load. Follow the approved switching programme and permit to work, use interlocks as designed, and operate HV equipment only if authorised and trained.

quiz.q: What is the main function of an isolator?
options: To provide a safe isolating gap
quiz.why: It provides isolation, usually without breaking load current.

quiz.q: When should a disconnector be opened?
options: With the breaker closed and on load
quiz.why: A disconnector is operated off load, after the breaker has opened the circuit.

quiz.q: What does an earthing switch do?
options: Connects isolated equipment to earth for safety
quiz.why: It earths the isolated section so it cannot become live unexpectedly.

summary: Breaker breaks load; isolator isolates.
Operate isolators with the breaker open.
Earth the isolated equipment and use interlocks and permits.

practice.q: Why is the earthing switch closed only after proving the equipment dead?
practice.a: Closing it onto a live section would create a short circuit to earth.

refs: IEC 60947-3 (switches, disconnectors, switch-disconnectors and fuse-combination units)
IEC 62271-102 (alternating current disconnectors and earthing switches)
Your site or utility switching and permit procedures

lessons.title: Current Transformers and Voltage Transformers
lessons.prereq: Three-Phase Systems; Active, Reactive and Apparent Power
objectives: Explain why CTs and VTs are used
Read a CT or VT ratio
Calculate secondary values and burden
State the critical safety rules for CT and VT secondaries
explain: Meters and relays cannot be connected directly to a high-voltage line carrying thousands of amperes. Instrument transformers give them a small, safe, accurate copy of the primary quantity.
A CT steps the current down (for example 400 A to 5 A). A VT steps the voltage down (for example 11 kV to 110 V).
lessons.definition: A current transformer (CT) delivers a secondary current proportional to the primary current; a voltage transformer (VT, also called PT) delivers a secondary voltage proportional to the primary voltage (IEC 61869 series). The ratio is written as primary/secondary, for example 400/5 A or 11 000/110 V. The burden is the load on the secondary, in VA. Metering classes (such as 0.5 or 0.2S) and protection classes (such as 5P20) describe accuracy. 5P20 means a composite error of at most 5 % at 20 times the rated current, at rated burden.

formulas.note: Example: 400/5 A gives a ratio of 80
R includes lead resistance and the device burden
VT ratio, for example 11 000 / 110 = 100

example.question: (a) A 400/5 A CT carries a primary current of 320 A. Find the secondary current. (b) The secondary circuit has lead resistance of 0.2 Ω and a relay that burdens 1 VA at 5 A. Find the total burden. (c) A VT of ratio 11 000/110 V reads 108.9 V on its secondary. Find the primary voltage.
steps: (b) Relay resistance = 1 / 5² = 0.04 Ω; total R = 0.2 + 0.04 = 0.24 Ω; burden = 5² × 0.24 = 6 VA

applications: CTs feed overcurrent, differential and distance relays and energy meters.
VTs feed voltage, frequency and directional elements and synchronising schemes.
CT and VT ratios and polarity are checked in commissioning before protection is put in service.
mistakes: Connecting a relay with the wrong CT polarity, which can cause maloperation of directional and differential protection.
Ignoring the burden. Too high a burden can make a CT saturate and give wrong readings.
Mixing up CT and VT rules when working on secondaries.
lessons.safety: Never open-circuit the secondary of an energised CT: it can produce a dangerously high voltage. Short the CT secondary using the proper shorting link or test block before disconnecting a burden. Never short-circuit the secondary of a VT, because it can overheat and fail.

quiz.q: A CT is 400/5 A and carries 200 A. What is its secondary current?
What must you never do with an energised CT secondary?
quiz.why: An open CT secondary can develop a dangerously high voltage.

quiz.q: What does the 5P20 class mean?
options: 5 % error at 20 times rated current at rated burden
quiz.why: 5P20: composite error up to 5 % at an accuracy limit factor of 20.

summary: CT: current ratio (e.g. 400/5). VT: voltage ratio (e.g. 11 000/110).
Burden in VA includes leads and devices.
CT secondary: never open. VT secondary: never short.

practice.q: A 200/1 A CT carries 150 A. Find the secondary current.

refs: IEC 61869-1 and IEC 61869-2 (instrument transformers: general requirements; current transformers)
IEC 61869-3 (inductive voltage transformers)
CT and VT nameplates and datasheets for class, burden and knee-point data

lessons.title: Energy Meters and Measuring Instruments
lessons.prereq: Power and Energy; Basic Electrical Measurements
objectives: Explain how energy meters record kWh
Use the meter constant to check a load
Understand accuracy class
Name common analogue and digital instrument types and their uses
explain: An energy meter is a kind of odometer for electricity. It adds up power over time and displays energy in kilowatt-hours.
Older electromechanical meters turn a disc; modern static meters sample voltage and current electronically and send pulses or digital readings. Large installations connect meters through CTs and VTs.
lessons.definition: An energy meter integrates power over time. Its meter constant relates registration to energy, for example 1600 revolutions per kWh or 1000 impulses per kWh. Accuracy class gives the permitted percentage error under reference conditions (for example class 1 means ±1 %). Static meters are covered by the IEC 62052 and 62053 series (for example IEC 62053-21 for classes 1 and 2 and IEC 62053-22 for classes 0.1S, 0.2S and 0.5S). Common instruments: moving-coil (DC), moving-iron (AC and DC RMS), dynamometer (power), and digital multimeters and power analysers.

formulas.f: E (kWh) = number of revolutions or impulses / meter constant
formulas.note: Meter constant in rev/kWh or imp/kWh
Average power over the test time
Under the reference conditions of the standard

example.question: (a) The disc of a 1600 rev/kWh meter makes 20 revolutions in 60 s. Find the load. (b) A 2 kW load is connected to a meter of 1000 imp/kWh. How many impulses per minute are expected?
steps: (b) 2 kW for 1 h = 2 kWh = 2000 impulses per hour

applications: Utilities use energy meters for billing; sub-meters allocate energy inside an installation.
Technicians check a meter by timing the disc or impulse LED against a known load.
Power analysers record voltage, current, power factor and harmonics for energy audits.
mistakes: Mixing kW (power) and kWh (energy).
Forgetting the CT and VT multiplying factor when a meter is connected through instrument transformers.
Reading an error limit as valid at any condition. It applies only at the reference conditions.
lessons.safety: Meter terminals and CT secondaries can be live or hazardous. Only authorised persons should open sealed meters or work on metering circuits, and CT secondaries must never be opened while the primary is energised.

quiz.q: A meter has a constant of 1000 imp/kWh. How many impulses represent 2.5 kWh?
quiz.why: 2.5 kWh × 1000 imp/kWh = 2500 impulses.

quiz.q: A class 1 meter has an allowed error of…
quiz.why: Class 1 means ±1 % under reference conditions.

quiz.q: Which instrument type reads true RMS of AC in a simple analogue form?
quiz.why: Moving-iron instruments respond to the RMS value and work on AC and DC.

summary: Energy = power × time; meter constant converts counts to kWh.
Class gives the permitted error at reference conditions.
Allow for CT and VT multiplying factors.

practice.q: A 1200 rev/kWh meter makes 30 revolutions in 90 s. Find the load.

refs: IEC 62052-11 and IEC 62053-21 / 62053-22 (electricity metering equipment): confirm the current editions
Your electricity supplier or regulator metering requirements

lessons.title: Cables
objectives: Describe the parts of a power cable
Compare PVC and XLPE insulation
Explain current-carrying capacity and derating
Apply the rule design current ≤ device rating ≤ cable capacity
explain: A cable is a conductor wrapped in insulation, with layers for protection. The conductor carries current, the insulation keeps it apart from other voltages, and the sheath protects against damage.

Every cable heats up as current flows. How much current it can carry depends on how well it can lose that heat: the insulation limit, the ambient temperature, and how many cables are grouped together.
lessons.definition: A power cable consists of conductors (copper or aluminium, IEC 60228), insulation (commonly PVC with a maximum conductor temperature of 70 °C, or XLPE at 90 °C), and bedding, armour and sheath as needed (for example IEC 60502 for power cables). The current-carrying capacity Iz is taken from tables in the applicable wiring rules (for example IEC 60364-5-52 or the local code) and reduced by correction factors for ambient temperature and grouping.

formulas.note: Correction factors come from the applicable standard
Design current ≤ protective device rating ≤ corrected cable capacity

formulas.f: Voltage drop = I × R × length (and reactance for larger cables)
formulas.note: Check against the allowed limit in your rules

example.question: A load draws a design current of 28 A. For illustration, assume a chosen cable has a tabulated capacity of 41 A, an ambient-temperature factor of 0.87 and a grouping factor of 0.8. Is the cable suitable, and what is the largest protective device rating allowed?
steps: Ib = 28 A is less than 28.5 A, so the cable is just adequate
The device rating In must satisfy 28 ≤ In ≤ 28.5, which leaves little margin, so a larger cable should be considered
example.answer: Iz = 28.5 A: marginal. These figures are illustrative, not taken from a standard.

applications: Choosing cable size for feeders, motors and panels.
Checking that a cable can carry load current and withstand fault current for the protection operating time.
Selecting the cable type for buried, tray or conduit installation.
mistakes: Using the tabulated capacity without applying temperature and grouping factors.
Choosing a cable only by current and ignoring voltage drop and short-circuit withstand.
Mixing copper and aluminium data.
lessons.safety: A damaged or overloaded cable can overheat, ignite or become live where it should not be. Do not exceed ratings, protect cables from mechanical damage, and treat every cable as live until isolated and proved dead.

quiz.q: Which insulation usually allows the higher maximum conductor temperature?
quiz.why: XLPE is commonly rated at 90 °C, PVC at 70 °C.

quiz.q: Grouping cables together does what to the current rating?
quiz.why: Grouped cables heat each other, so a correction factor below 1 applies.

quiz.q: Which condition is correct for protection?
quiz.why: The device rating lies between the design current and the corrected cable capacity.

summary: Cable capacity falls with temperature and grouping.
Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz.
Also check voltage drop and short-circuit withstand.

practice.q: Table value 32 A, temperature factor 0.94, grouping factor 0.7. Find Iz.

refs: IEC 60364-5-52 (selection and erection of wiring systems) or the wiring code that applies where you work
IEC 60228 (conductors) and the IEC 60502 series (power cables)
Cable manufacturer datasheets: confirm the current editions

lessons.title: Busbars
objectives: Explain what a busbar is and why copper or aluminium is used
Estimate busbar resistance and heat loss
Explain the force between busbars during a short circuit
List key busbar design and maintenance points
explain: A busbar is a solid metal bar that acts as a main junction where many circuits connect. It carries large currents with less heat than many separate cables.
During a short circuit the huge current also pushes and pulls the bars with great force, so busbars and their supports must be strong as well as conductive.
lessons.definition: A busbar is a conductor, usually of copper or aluminium, used to collect and distribute electrical power inside switchgear and panels. Resistance is R = ρL / A, and the heat produced is I²R. Parallel conductors carrying current exert a force per metre of F/L = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × I² / d (newtons per metre, with I in amperes and spacing d in metres) for two long parallel conductors carrying the same current. Low-voltage assemblies are covered by IEC 61439.

formulas.note: Copper ρ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m; aluminium ρ ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m
Watts per bar for the given length
Force per metre between two parallel conductors, I in A, d in m

example.question: (a) A copper busbar is 50 mm × 10 mm and 1 m long. Find its resistance and its heat loss at 800 A. Compare with an aluminium bar of the same size. (b) Two parallel bars 100 mm apart each carry 10 kA. Find the force per metre.
example.answer: (a) copper 21.8 W, aluminium 35.8 W   (b) 200 N per metre (real fault peaks can be higher)

applications: Switchboards and panels use busbars as incoming and outgoing distribution points.
Substations use busbars at various voltages with specific arrangements (covered later in Power Systems).
Thermographic scans find hot joints on busbars during maintenance.
mistakes: Ignoring joints: a loose or oxidised joint raises resistance and causes overheating.
Sizing only for continuous current and ignoring short-circuit forces.
Using too small a clearance, which risks flashover.
lessons.safety: Busbars can be live behind covers and carry very large fault energy. Isolate, prove dead, earth and follow permit procedures. Never open covers or inspect busbars while energised unless authorised, trained and using the correct arc-flash precautions.

quiz.q: Which has the lower resistivity, copper or aluminium?
quiz.why: Copper is about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m and aluminium about 2.8 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m.

quiz.q: What causes heating at a busbar joint?
quiz.why: A poor joint adds resistance, and heat is I²R.

quiz.q: If the fault current doubles, the force between parallel bars becomes…
quiz.why: F is proportional to I², so doubling I gives four times the force.

summary: R = ρL / A and heat = I²R.
Copper conducts better than aluminium; aluminium is lighter.
Fault force is proportional to I² and must be withstood by the supports.

practice.q: A copper bar of 100 mm × 10 mm and 2 m length carries 1000 A. Find its heat loss.

lessons.title: Transformers and Motors: Overview
lessons.prereq: Three-Phase Systems; Active, Reactive and Apparent Power
objectives: Explain the basic principle of a transformer
Calculate transformer rated currents from kVA
Explain synchronous speed and slip in an induction motor
Recognise why transformers are rated in kVA
explain: A transformer moves energy between two circuits with no electrical connection, using a magnetic field in an iron core. It changes voltage and current but not frequency.
An induction motor makes a rotating magnetic field in the stator. The rotor chases that field but runs slightly slower, and the difference is called slip.
lessons.definition: A transformer works by mutual induction. For an ideal transformer V1 / V2 = N1 / N2 = I2 / I1, and its rating is in kVA. The synchronous speed of the rotating field is Ns = 120 × f / P (rpm, with P poles). An induction motor runs at a speed N below Ns, and slip is s = (Ns − N) / Ns. Detailed theory, equivalent circuits and testing follow in Path 03.

formulas.note: Ideal transformer
Three-phase rated line current from kVA

formulas.f: Ns = 120 f / P   s = (Ns − N) / Ns
formulas.note: Induction motor speed and slip

example.question: (a) A 100 kVA, 11 kV / 415 V three-phase transformer: find the rated primary and secondary currents. (b) A 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 1450 rpm. Find the synchronous speed and slip.
example.answer: (a) 5.25 A and 139.1 A   (b) 1500 rpm and 3.33 % slip

applications: Distribution transformers step 11 kV down to 415 V for consumers.
Induction motors drive pumps, fans, compressors and conveyors.
The nameplate gives kVA, voltage ratio, vector group, speed and current.
mistakes: Rating a transformer in kW instead of kVA.
Forgetting slip: the motor does not run at synchronous speed.
Mixing line and phase quantities.
lessons.safety: Transformers can back-feed from the low-voltage side and stay energised or hold charge. Rotating machines can restart unexpectedly. Isolate, lock off, prove dead and earth before work.

quiz.q: Why are transformers rated in kVA?
options: Losses depend on voltage and current, not power factor
kW is not an SI unit
quiz.why: Heating depends on V and I, so the kVA rating applies for any power factor.

quiz.q: What is the synchronous speed of a 2-pole machine at 50 Hz?
A motor with Ns = 1500 rpm runs at 1470 rpm. What is the slip?

summary: Ideal transformer: V1/V2 = N1/N2 = I2/I1.
Ns = 120f/P; slip = (Ns − N)/Ns.
Full theory and testing come in Path 03.

lessons.title: Generators
lessons.prereq: Transformers and Motors: Overview; Three-Phase Systems
objectives: Describe how a synchronous generator produces three-phase voltage
Relate frequency, speed and number of poles
Explain how voltage and frequency are controlled
Understand kVA, kW and rated current of a generator
explain: A generator turns mechanical energy into electrical energy. A DC current in the rotor makes a magnet, the rotor is turned by an engine or turbine, and its moving field induces voltage in the stator windings.
The speed fixes the frequency and the excitation fixes the voltage. That is why generators have a governor for speed and an automatic voltage regulator (AVR) for excitation.
lessons.definition: A synchronous generator (alternator) has a DC-excited rotor and a three-phase stator winding. Its frequency is f = P × N / 120, with P poles and N rpm. Increasing excitation raises the terminal voltage; the governor sets speed and hence frequency. The rating is in kVA at a stated power factor, and the real power is P = S × pf. To run in parallel with a supply, voltage, frequency, phase sequence and phase angle must match.

formulas.note: f in Hz, N in rpm, P number of poles
Real power output from the rating
Rated line current

example.question: (a) A 500 kVA, 415 V, 0.8 power factor generator: find its rated real power and rated line current. (b) How many poles give 50 Hz at 750 rpm?

applications: Diesel generator sets provide standby power in buildings and plants.
Turbine generators in power stations feed the grid.
Solar and wind systems use inverters instead of rotating synchronous machines in many designs.
mistakes: Mixing up kVA and kW on a generator rating.
Closing a generator onto a live supply out of synchronism.
Forgetting that speed changes frequency and excitation changes voltage.
lessons.safety: A generator can back-feed into a supply and endanger line workers. Use proper changeover and interlocking, and isolate and lock off before work. Rotating machines, exhaust gases, fuel and noise are also hazards.

quiz.q: What does the governor control?
quiz.why: The governor controls prime-mover speed, which sets frequency.

quiz.q: A 6-pole machine runs at 1000 rpm. What is the frequency?
A 250 kVA generator has a 0.8 power factor rating. What is its kW rating?

summary: Excitation controls voltage; the governor controls frequency.
Rated in kVA; kW = kVA × pf.

practice.q: Find the frequency of a 4-pole generator at 1500 rpm.

lessons.title: Capacitor Banks and Reactors
lessons.prereq: Power Factor and Correction; Impedance, Resonance and Power Factor
objectives: Calculate the capacitance and current of a capacitor bank
Explain why detuning reactors are used with capacitors
Name the main reactor types and what they do
explain: A capacitor bank supplies reactive power locally, as you saw in power factor correction. A reactor does the opposite job: it adds inductance to limit current, filter harmonics or absorb reactive power.
Capacitors and the network inductance can resonate. A series reactor with the capacitor moves that resonance to a frequency where there is no harmonic problem.
lessons.definition: A three-phase capacitor bank of rating Qc (kvar) connected in delta has a capacitance per phase C = Qc / (3 × 2πf × V²), with V the line voltage. A detuned filter places a series reactor of p % reactance with the capacitor, giving a series resonance at f(r) = f / √p. Shunt reactors absorb reactive power and limit voltage rise on lightly loaded lines; series (current-limiting) reactors limit fault current; neutral earthing reactors limit earth-fault current.

formulas.f: Qc = √3 × VL × IL   C(Δ) = Qc / (3 × ω × VL²)
formulas.note: Bank rating and delta capacitance per phase
Series resonance of a detuned bank; p is the reactor fraction (for example 0.07 for 7 %)
Choose to suit the harmonics present

example.question: (a) A 50 kvar, 415 V, 50 Hz bank is connected in delta. Find the line current and capacitance per phase. (b) A 7 % detuning reactor is used. Find the series resonant frequency.
example.answer: (a) 69.6 A and about 308 µF per phase   (b) about 189 Hz (below the 5th harmonic at 250 Hz)

applications: Automatic power factor correction panels switch capacitor steps to follow the load.
Detuning reactors protect capacitor banks in networks with harmonics.
Current-limiting reactors protect equipment from high fault currents; shunt reactors help control voltage on long lines.
mistakes: Connecting a capacitor bank where harmonics are strong without a detuning reactor.
Switching a bank back on before it has discharged.
Confusing a shunt reactor (voltage control) with a series reactor (current limiting).
lessons.safety: Capacitor banks keep a dangerous charge after isolation. Wait for the discharge time stated by the manufacturer, prove dead and earth before touching. Banks can also fail violently if over-stressed.

quiz.q: What unit is used to rate a capacitor bank?
quiz.why: Capacitors supply reactive power in kvar.

quiz.q: Where does a 7 % detuned filter resonate at 50 Hz?
What is the main job of a shunt reactor?
options: Absorb reactive power and limit voltage rise
quiz.why: It absorbs reactive power, often on lightly loaded lines.

summary: Qc = √3 VL IL; C(Δ) = Qc / (3ωVL²).
Detuning: f(r) = f / √p.
Reactor types: shunt, series (current limiting) and neutral earthing.

practice.q: A 14 % detuning reactor on a 50 Hz network: find the series resonant frequency.

lessons.title: UPS and Battery Systems
lessons.prereq: Power and Energy; Diodes, Transistors and Basic Electronic Components
objectives: Compare standby, line-interactive and double-conversion UPS
Estimate battery energy and backup time
Describe common battery types and their hazards
explain: A UPS (uninterruptible power supply) keeps critical loads running through a mains failure. A battery stores the energy, and electronics (rectifier, inverter) turn it into AC for the load.
Substation protection and control systems use a similar idea at DC: a charger keeps a battery floating so that relays and breaker coils always have power, even if the AC supply is lost.
lessons.definition: A UPS contains a rectifier-charger, a battery and an inverter. Standby (offline), line-interactive and online double-conversion types differ in how the load is supplied in normal operation (IEC 62040-3 classifies them). Battery capacity is rated in ampere-hours (Ah), and the stored energy is E = V × Ah. Backup time is approximately the usable energy divided by the load power, reduced by depth of discharge and efficiency. Float and boost charge voltages must follow the battery manufacturer data.

formulas.note: Stored energy of the battery bank

formulas.f: Backup time (h) ≈ E × DoD × η / P(load)
formulas.note: DoD = usable fraction; η = inverter efficiency. A rough estimate only
Battery current from the load

example.question: A UPS has a 192 V, 100 Ah battery bank. With a usable fraction of 0.8 and an inverter efficiency of 0.9, estimate the backup time for a 3 kW load and the battery current.
example.answer: About 4.6 h and 17.4 A. Real battery capacity is lower at higher discharge rates, so check the manufacturer discharge tables.

applications: UPS systems back up computers, control rooms, SCADA and communications equipment.
Substation DC systems (battery and charger) power protection relays, trip coils and closing circuits.
Battery banks need regular inspection, testing and capacity checks.
mistakes: Using the nameplate Ah without allowing for the discharge rate and ageing.
Choosing a UPS by kW only and ignoring kVA and inrush.
Ignoring battery ventilation and temperature.
lessons.safety: Batteries can deliver very high short-circuit currents. Flooded lead-acid cells give off hydrogen, so keep them ventilated and free of sparks, and acid is corrosive. Lithium batteries can overheat. A UPS and its battery can still be live after the mains is isolated, so isolate the battery as well and prove dead.

quiz.q: Which UPS type supplies the load through the inverter all the time?
quiz.why: Double-conversion supplies the load through the inverter continuously.

quiz.q: A 48 V, 200 Ah battery stores about…
Why must flooded lead-acid batteries be ventilated?
quiz.why: Charging releases hydrogen, which is explosive in the right concentration.

summary: UPS = rectifier, battery and inverter.
E = V × Ah / 1000; backup time is about usable energy / load.
Batteries carry high fault current and gas hazards.

practice.q: A 24 V, 100 Ah battery with 0.5 usable fraction and 0.9 efficiency supplies 600 W. Estimate the time.

Battery manufacturer discharge tables and float voltage data

lessons.title: Nameplate Interpretation
lessons.prereq: Transformers and Motors: Overview; Basic Electrical Measurements
objectives: Find and read the key ratings on a motor nameplate
Check a nameplate for consistency using simple calculations
Understand IP codes and insulation class
explain: A nameplate is the equipment's identity card. It tells you what voltage, current and duty the maker designed it for, and it is the first thing to read before connecting, testing or replacing anything.
Always compare the nameplate with the supply, the cable, the protection settings and the drawings.
lessons.definition: The nameplate lists the rated values at which the equipment is designed to operate. A motor nameplate typically shows rated output power (kW), voltage and winding connection (Y or Δ), rated current, frequency, speed (rpm), power factor (cosφ), duty type (S1 is continuous duty), insulation class and the IP code. The IP code (IEC 60529) has two digits: the first for protection against solid objects and dust, the second for protection against water. Thermal classes (IEC 60085) set the maximum temperature: B 130 °C, F 155 °C, H 180 °C.

formulas.note: Round the rated speed up to the nearest synchronous speed to find the poles

formulas.f: P(in) = √3 × V × I × cosφ   η = P(out) / P(in)
formulas.note: Implied efficiency from nameplate values

formulas.f: IP5x: dust protected   IPx5: water jets
formulas.note: Example: IP55 has both digits 5

example.question: An illustrative motor nameplate reads: 11 kW, 415 V, 50 Hz, 20.5 A, cosφ 0.86, 1460 rpm, S1, insulation class F, IP55. Find the number of poles, the slip, and the efficiency implied by the other values.
steps: Rated speed 1460 rpm is just below 1500 rpm, so Ns = 1500 rpm and poles = 120 × 50 / 1500 = 4

applications: Before connecting a motor, check that the nameplate voltage and connection match the supply and the starter.
Overload relays are set from the nameplate full-load current.
Replacement equipment is chosen by matching the nameplate ratings and frame size.
mistakes: Reading only the kW and ignoring voltage, connection and duty.
Setting the overload relay from the supply current instead of the nameplate current.
Assuming IP rating covers every environment. Check the actual dust and water conditions.
lessons.safety: A wrong supply voltage or winding connection can overheat or burn out a motor. Check the nameplate and the connection diagram before energising, and isolate before changing the connections.

quiz.q: A nameplate shows 1460 rpm at 50 Hz. How many poles has the motor?
quiz.why: The synchronous speed just above 1460 rpm is 1500 rpm, which is 4 poles.

quiz.q: In IP55, what does the second digit show?
quiz.why: The second digit is protection against water.

quiz.q: Which insulation class has the highest maximum temperature?
quiz.why: H allows 180 °C, F 155 °C and B 130 °C.

summary: Read ratings, connection, duty, IP and insulation class.
Poles from speed; slip from rated and synchronous speed.
Match the nameplate to supply, cable and protection.

practice.q: A 6-pole 50 Hz motor shows 960 rpm. What is the slip?

lessons.title: Ratings, Applications and Limitations
objectives: Explain what a rating means and how it can be exceeded
Calculate loading and margin against a rating
Explain derating for environment
Name the limits of common devices
explain: A rating is a promise with conditions. A 63 A breaker or a 500 kVA transformer is only rated for those values at the conditions the maker assumed, such as ambient temperature, altitude and duty.
Running at the rating all the time leaves no margin. Good practice is to know the loading, the margin to the limit, and what happens when the conditions change.
lessons.definition: A rating is the value of a quantity assigned to equipment for specified operating conditions. Continuous ratings assume steady operation; short-time and overload ratings are limited in duration. Ambient temperature, altitude, harmonics and grouping can require derating, with factors taken from the manufacturer or the applicable standard. Fault ratings (such as breaking capacity and short-time withstand) must be at least equal to the fault level at the installation point.

formulas.note: Transformer or generator loading
For example breaking capacity minus prospective fault current
The factor comes from the manufacturer data or the standard

example.question: (a) A 500 kVA transformer supplies a 360 kW load at power factor 0.8. Find the loading. (b) A breaker has a breaking capacity of 25 kA and the prospective fault current is 18 kA. Find the margin. (c) A 63 A device needs a derating factor of 0.9 for ambient temperature (assumed here for illustration). Find the usable current.

applications: Checking loading before adding new load to a transformer or feeder.
Comparing fault level with breaker and busbar ratings after a network change.
Selecting equipment for hot, dusty or high-altitude sites.
mistakes: Treating the rating as the normal operating value with no margin.
Ignoring the ambient temperature or altitude assumed by the manufacturer.
Comparing a continuous current rating with a short-time or starting current.
lessons.safety: Operating beyond ratings shortens life and can cause failure, fire or arc faults. Do not increase protection settings to stop nuisance tripping without finding the cause.

quiz.q: A 500 kVA transformer carries 450 kVA. What is the loading?
Which fault rating must be at least the prospective fault current?
quiz.why: The breaking capacity must cover the fault level at the installation point.

quiz.q: Why is a device derated in a hot ambient?
options: Its temperature limit is reached sooner
quiz.why: Less heat can be lost, so a lower current keeps temperatures within limits.

summary: A rating applies under stated conditions.
Check loading, margin and fault ratings.
Derate for ambient, altitude and grouping per the manufacturer or standard.

practice.q: A 250 kVA transformer carries 180 kW at pf 0.9. Find the loading.

lessons.title: Common Failure Modes
lessons.prereq: Ratings, Applications and Limitations; Power and Energy
objectives: List the common causes of electrical equipment failure
Describe typical failure modes of motors, transformers, breakers, cables, capacitors and batteries
Explain the bathtub curve
Use failure rate, MTBF and a simple reliability calculation
explain: Equipment rarely fails without a warning sign. Heat, noise, vibration, smell, discolouration and tripping are the early clues.
Most failures start from a few causes: overheating, insulation ageing, moisture, contamination, mechanical wear and loose connections. Knowing the pattern helps you find the cause faster.
lessons.definition: A failure mode is the way in which equipment fails to perform its function. Typical examples: motors (bearing wear, winding insulation breakdown, single-phasing), transformers (insulation ageing, oil contamination, overloading, bushing faults), breakers (contact wear, failure to trip or close), cables (insulation breakdown, joint failure), capacitors (dielectric failure), contactors (welded contacts, coil burn-out) and batteries (capacity loss, sulphation). The failure rate λ is the number of failures per unit time; for a constant rate MTBF = 1 / λ and reliability R(t) = e^(−λt).

formulas.note: Mean time between failures for a constant failure rate
Probability of operating without failure for time t

formulas.f: Loss in a poor joint = I² × R(joint)
formulas.note: Excess contact resistance produces heat

example.question: (a) A component has a constant failure rate of 0.0002 per hour. Find its MTBF and the probability of surviving 1000 hours. (b) A poor joint adds 5 mΩ to a circuit carrying 100 A. Find the heat produced.
example.answer: (a) 5000 h; 81.9 % chance of surviving 1000 h   (b) 50 W, enough to overheat a terminal

applications: Thermography finds hot joints before they fail.
Oil tests and winding resistance tests track transformer health.
Regular inspection and testing of breakers and relays catch hidden failures.
mistakes: Replacing a failed part without finding the root cause.
Re-energising after a protection trip without investigation.
Treating a constant failure rate as valid for wear-out failures.
lessons.safety: Investigate failures only after isolating and proving dead. Failed equipment may be hot, pressurised or contain stored energy. Never reset a protection trip repeatedly to test whether the fault has cleared.

quiz.q: What does a loose electrical connection mainly cause?
quiz.why: The extra resistance dissipates I²R as heat.

quiz.q: A failure rate is 0.001 per hour. What is the MTBF?
Which part of the bathtub curve has a roughly constant failure rate?
quiz.why: The flat middle section is the useful life.

summary: Most failures start with heat, insulation ageing, moisture, wear or loose joints.
MTBF = 1/λ and R(t) = e^(−λt).
Find the root cause before re-energising.

practice.q: λ = 0.0005 per hour. Find the MTBF.

lessons.title: Equipment Selection Fundamentals
lessons.prereq: Failure Modes; Contactors and Auxiliary Relays; Cables
objectives: Follow a step-by-step selection process
Work out the full-load current of a motor from its rating
Check starting current, fault level and environment
Document the selection
explain: Selecting equipment is answering the same questions every time: what does it have to do, what rating does that need, what can go wrong, and where will it live?
Good selection is a short, repeatable checklist, not a guess.
lessons.definition: Selection is the process of choosing equipment whose ratings, protection and construction suit the duty, the fault level, the environment and the applicable standards. The steps are: define the duty and environment; choose the rating with a margin; check the fault level and breaking capacity; check environment, standards and coordination; then select, document and plan maintenance.

formulas.note: Motor full-load current
k for a direct-on-line start is typically around 6 to 8; use the motor datasheet
Check the voltage, current, fault and environment ratings

example.question: Outline the selection for a 7.5 kW, 415 V three-phase motor with efficiency 0.88 and power factor 0.85, started direct-on-line.
steps: Assume a starting current of 7 × 13.9 ≈ 97 A for this check (use the motor datasheet)
Contactor: AC-3 rating at 415 V of at least 14 A (check manufacturer tables)
Overload relay: adjustment range that includes 13.9 A
Short-circuit device: must not trip on the 97 A starting current and must have a breaking capacity above the fault level
Cable: current capacity above 13.9 A after derating, and acceptable voltage drop
example.answer: FLC 13.9 A; start about 97 A (assumed 7×); contactor AC-3 ≥ 14 A; check protection and cable

applications: Specifying equipment for a new panel or feeder.
Checking that replacement equipment is a valid substitute.
Preparing a bill of quantities with correct ratings.
mistakes: Selecting by kW or current alone and ignoring fault level and environment.
Forgetting starting current and duty cycle.
Not recording the assumptions, so the next engineer cannot check the choice.
lessons.safety: Selection calculations here are educational. Final selection must use the manufacturer data, the applicable standards and the approval of a qualified engineer.

quiz.q: Which step comes first in selection?
quiz.why: You must know the duty before you can choose a rating.

quiz.q: A motor has an FLC of 13.9 A. Which contactor AC-3 rating is suitable?
quiz.why: The AC-3 rating must be at least the full-load current.

quiz.q: Why record the assumptions?
options: So the choice can be checked later
quiz.why: Recorded assumptions make the selection reviewable.

summary: Define duty, choose rating, check fault level, check environment and standards, document.
Use FLC and starting current for motors.
Use manufacturer data for the final choice.

lessons.title: Magnetic Circuits
lessons.prereq: Resistance, Inductance and Capacitance; Ohm's Law
objectives: Define flux, flux density, mmf and reluctance
Use the magnetic circuit equation
Show how an air gap affects flux
Explain saturation and core losses
explain: Current in a coil creates a magnetic field. An iron core guides that field, like a wire guides current. The magnetic circuit is analysed in the same way as an electrical one.
Think of mmf as the driving "voltage", flux as the "current" and reluctance as the "resistance" of the magnetic path.
lessons.definition: Magnetic flux Φ is measured in weber (Wb) and flux density is B = Φ / A in tesla (T). The magnetomotive force of a coil is mmf = N × I (ampere-turns). Reluctance is S = l / (μ0 μr A), where μ0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m, and Φ = mmf / S. In a real core, permeability falls when the core saturates, and losses occur as hysteresis and eddy currents, which is why cores are laminated.

formulas.f: Φ = mmf / S = N I / S
formulas.note: Magnetic equivalent of Ohm's law
Reluctance in A/Wb; l in m, A in m²
Flux density in tesla

example.question: An iron ring has a mean length of 0.4 m, a cross-section of 4 cm² and μr = 1000. A 500-turn coil carries 0.5 A. (a) Find the flux and flux density. (b) A 1 mm air gap is cut in the ring. Find the new flux (ignore fringing).
example.answer: (a) Φ = 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ Wb, B = 0.785 T   (b) Φ = 8.98 × 10⁻⁵ Wb, B = 0.224 T: a 1 mm gap cuts the flux to about 29 %

applications: Transformer and motor cores guide the flux that carries energy.
CT cores can saturate at high fault currents, giving a distorted output.
Relays and contactors use electromagnets whose pull depends on the air gap.
mistakes: Assuming μr stays constant. At high flux the core saturates.
Forgetting the air gap, which dominates the reluctance.
Mixing cm² and m² in the area.
lessons.safety: Large magnetic fields can affect pacemakers and move tools. A CT with an open secondary can drive its core into deep saturation and produce a dangerous voltage, so never open an energised CT secondary.

quiz.q: What is the unit of flux density?
quiz.why: Flux density B is measured in tesla (Wb/m²).

quiz.q: A coil of 200 turns carries 2 A. What is the mmf?
quiz.why: mmf = N × I = 200 × 2 = 400 A-turns.

quiz.q: Why does a small air gap greatly reduce flux?
quiz.why: Air has a much higher reluctance than iron, so the gap dominates.

summary: Φ = mmf / S; S = l / (μ0 μr A); B = Φ / A.
An air gap dominates reluctance.
Cores saturate and are laminated to reduce eddy-current loss.

lessons.title: Transformer Construction and Operation
lessons.prereq: Magnetic Circuits; Transformers and Motors: Overview
objectives: Name the main parts of a power transformer
Use the EMF equation E = 4.44 f N Φm
Explain why flux depends on V/f
Describe common cooling types
explain: A transformer has two windings on a laminated iron core. Alternating current in the primary creates a changing flux in the core, and that flux induces voltage in the secondary.
Oil-filled power transformers add a tank, oil for insulation and cooling, bushings to bring conductors out, and fittings that watch over the oil.
lessons.definition: The core is made of laminated silicon steel to reduce eddy-current loss. The windings are copper or aluminium, with the low-voltage (LV) winding usually nearest the core and the high-voltage (HV) winding outside it. The EMF equation for an RMS voltage is E = 4.44 × f × N × Φm. Because Φm = E / (4.44 f N), the core flux depends on the ratio of voltage to frequency. Oil-immersed transformers use a conservator, a breather and often a Buchholz relay; cooling designations such as ONAN (oil natural, air natural) are defined in IEC 60076-2.

formulas.note: RMS EMF; f in Hz, Φm in Wb (peak flux)
Peak flux set by the voltage and frequency
Peak flux density in the core

example.question: A transformer winding of 1000 turns is supplied at 11 kV, 50 Hz. The core cross-section is 0.05 m². Find the peak flux, the peak flux density, and the secondary turns for 415 V.
example.answer: Φm ≈ 0.0495 Wb, Bm ≈ 0.99 T, about 38 secondary turns

applications: Distribution and power transformers step voltages up and down in the grid.
The conservator and Buchholz relay give early warning of oil and internal faults.
Over-fluxing from high voltage or low frequency is detected by volts-per-hertz protection.
mistakes: Applying DC to a transformer. It does not transform and can overheat the winding.
Confusing which winding is HV and which is LV.
Forgetting that a lower frequency raises the flux for the same voltage.
lessons.safety: Transformer oil is flammable and hot oil can cause burns. Transformers can stay charged and can back-feed. Isolate, prove dead and earth. Do not open the conservator or sample oil without the approved procedure.

quiz.q: Why is a transformer core laminated?
quiz.why: Thin insulated laminations cut eddy currents.

quiz.q: Peak flux in a transformer is proportional to…
quiz.why: Φm = E / (4.44 f N), so flux depends on V/f.

quiz.q: What does ONAN mean?
quiz.why: ONAN is oil natural, air natural cooling.

summary: Core, windings, insulation and tank; conservator, breather and Buchholz on oil units.
E = 4.44 f N Φm.
Flux depends on V/f.
